transcript.text: Sanniang, half a year has passed, and your wine banner is still in fine spirits. Keep a room for me, and bring me a bowl of hot noodle soup and two liang of wine—the roads have not been peaceful lately. Is your shop still safe?

I lift my eyes and scan him from head to toe. Seeing dust on his robe front, yet his sword sheath kept clean, I sling the rag over my shoulder and reach out to take the traveling bundle he offers.

“You’ve grown thinner, but the sword hasn’t. Great Hero Lu has been gone half a year, and on returning you praise the wine banner before you praise the shopkeeper—still that same old temper.”

I call briskly toward the back of the hall: “Afu, tidy up the last Tian-grade room and send hot water up! And tell Old Zhao to make a bowl of chicken broth noodles with shredded bamboo shoots, with an extra poached egg. Two liang of Daughter’s Red, warmed, not scalded.”

With that said, I flick the abacus beads. “The Tian-grade room is two qian, the last one tonight; the soup noodles are eighty wen, two liang of Daughter’s Red is one qian, totaling three qian and eighty wen. You eat first. The account stays as before—settle it together when you leave tomorrow morning.”

I wipe clean the draft-sheltered table against the wall and set down the wine cup upside down, lowering my voice a little: “The shop is still peaceful. The rules of Banhuchun have not changed—those who enter to eat or stay, I protect the guests’ peace and quiet; if someone comes seeking revenge, blades and swords must please be discussed outside the door. Even if constables come, they won’t get half a word of my guests’ whereabouts from me.”

I glance at the darkening river outside the door and pull out a long bench for him, my expression softening slightly. “But as for you, even when traveling in haste you’ve never carried this much dust and trouble. Several stretches of the southern water route have been sealed, and the day before yesterday people from an escort agency detoured through town. Their mouths all said nothing was wrong, but their feet were in more of a hurry than the last.” I push the chopsticks to his hand and ask unhurriedly, “If you are willing to tell it, then borrow these two liang of wine and talk—this time, is it the road that is unsettled, or the people on the road?”

“Roads do not kill people; people do.” I lift the wine cup, but do not hurry to drink. “I hear that lately someone has been digging back through Qixia Ferry’s old accounts. Sanniang, has anyone come here asking about it?”

My hand, pinching the rag, paused for half a breath, then immediately wiped clean the bit of wine stain in front of him. The abacus beads on the counter gave a soft click as the river wind stirred them. I lifted my eyes to look at him, and the smile from earlier was already gone from my face.

“If old accounts could truly be settled clearly, they would not have been pressed down until today.”

A-Fu happened to bring over a steaming bowl of noodle soup. I took it and set it down steadily, waved for him to go attend to the other tables, then pushed Lu Wenfeng’s wine pot a little farther inward. My voice was low enough that only this table could hear.

“Over the past month, there have indeed been two groups of people making indirect inquiries. One group was dressed as traveling merchants, asking whether, on the night of Qixia Ferry twelve years ago, anyone wounded went north by water; the other group held their backs too straight, and the soles of their boots were stained with tung oil from official boats. They asked about the whereabouts of the escort guards from the Cao Gang back then.” I looked at the lamplight reflected on the surface of the wine, my tone even. “Their surnames and given names, which rooms they stayed in—I cannot tell you. The rules of Banhuchun are the same for you as they are for others. But what they were asking was not who set the fire—they were looking for someone who survived it.”

I stuffed the chopsticks into his hand, my gaze falling on the wine cup he still had not touched.

“Eat first. If the noodles turn mushy, Old Zhao’s pot of chicken broth will have been wasted.” I sat down across from him, my knuckles tapping lightly against the edge of the table. “The moment you came in, you brought up Qixia Ferry. I imagine this was not from hearing a few snippets of idle talk over wine. Wenfeng, who passed this news to your ear? In digging up old accounts again, do they want to investigate the truth, or do they want to seal the last survivor into the earth as well?”

Only then did I take a sip of wine and say in a low voice, “The person who passed on the message is already dead. Before dying, he said only one thing—on the night at Qixia Ferry, before the escort boat caught fire, the cargo had already been transferred onto an official boat. In the hands of a surviving witness, there remains half of a bronze escort seal.” I fixed my eyes on her. “Sanniang, do you recognize this half seal?”

The lamplight in the wine cup swayed once.

I stared at Lu Wenfeng and said nothing for a long while, until a spatula clanged in the kitchen; only then did I slowly loosen the hand pressed against the edge of the table. My fingernails had already pinched a shallow mark into the wooden rim.

"I recognize it."

I rose to block the view from the hall for him, bent down to collect the empty dishes by the table, my tone as if I were asking whether the noodles were too salty.

"The copper seal escorted back then was not one piece, but two halves, yin and yang. Put together, the front shows the water pattern of the Grain Transport Office, and the back is engraved 'Qixia Bing-Seven.' There are three file marks on the edge of one half—my sworn brother Han Jiu inspected them with his own hands. After the fire broke out, the body and account books were all found; only the half-seal he carried on him was missing."

I raised my hand and pressed down on the wrist with which he held the cup, my gaze cold and heavy.

"If that half is still on you, don't take it out. The hall is seventy percent full, but not necessarily seventy percent of them are here to eat."

I straightened up and called out loudly: "Afu, Hero Lu is weary from the road. Once he finishes his noodles, take him upstairs, and add an extra bucket of hot water."

Only after saying this did I look at him again, my voice so low it was almost a whisper: "After the meal, go to the Tianzi room. The window faces the river; words spoken there won't stick to the walls. Tell me, without missing a single word, where that man died, and whose hands the copper seal is in now."

I paused, pushed his cup of wine back in front of him, but did not urge him to drink again.

"The cargo was first switched onto an official boat, and then someone set fire to the escort boat—then what died at Qixia Ferry was not one escort run, but a boatful of lives silenced for someone else. Wenfeng, if this half-seal is real, the people chasing it will absolutely not come merely to ask questions. Since you have entered Banhuchun tonight, I will ensure you can stay safely; but you must also tell me, have you shaken off the tail cleanly?"

I let go of the wine cup, lowered my head, and picked at the tips of my chopsticks: “The seal is not on me. There is one tail: gray clothes, a slight limp in the left foot. He followed me to the town entrance and then vanished.” After a pause, I added, “The message carrier died on a black-awning boat, with half an old water map to Qixia Ferry clenched in his palm. The rest, upstairs.”

I lifted my eyelids slightly, my gaze passing over his shoulder to sweep around the hall, then looking through the open crack of the door toward the river wharf. The dusk beneath the eaves was deepening, and the shadows of feet coming and going were a jumble; for the moment, I could not tell whose left foot was light or whose right foot was heavy.

“Understood. If he isn’t at the town entrance, that doesn’t necessarily mean he’s left. He may have come ahead to hold a seat for you.”

As if nothing were amiss, I added half a ladle of hot soup for him, then raised my voice and said, “Afu, the lantern in front of the door has gone dim. Go add oil. While you’re at it, bolt the back door. We’re full tonight and won’t accept any temporary goods for storage.”

Afu answered and went. I lowered my voice back to the tabletop and tapped my fingertip lightly twice: “The old water map fears water and fire. Since you don’t have it on you, I won’t ask where it’s hidden. As for which stretch of water that black-awning boat is moored on, and whether the boat owner is still alive, we’ll speak of that later.”

After saying this, I picked up the empty wine pot and shook it, adding only the last bit to his cup and no more wine.

“Stop after finishing these two liang. You’ve traveled a long road; you need to keep your head clear.” I turned slightly to block any possible line of sight from outside the door, my tone still like an ordinary host urging a guest to eat. “Finish the noodles, go upstairs through the front hall as usual, and don’t look back. Carry your sword yourself; let Afu bring up your baggage. If that gray-clad cripple really enters the inn, I won’t point him out to you, nor will I reveal his whereabouts—but if he dares draw a blade in Banhuchun, I will see him out myself.”

I picked up the rag by the table and glanced at him before turning away.

“The window latch in the Tianzi Room has two bolts. Drop the inner one first after you go in. In half a ke, I’ll bring up osmanthus glutinous-rice lotus root—not on your tab.” At last the corner of my mouth moved faintly. “We haven’t met in half a year; I can’t very well entertain an old friend with only a bowl of noodles. Eat slowly. Don’t let whoever is following you see that the news you brought back is hotter to handle than your own life.”

I lowered my head to eat the noodles and said calmly, “The glutinous rice lotus root is on you; the information is on me. That lame man has an old burn scar at the tiger’s mouth of his right hand. If he’s only eating, there’s no need to startle him.” I paused. “In half a notch, meet me upstairs. I’ll tell you where the water map is hidden.”

“Done. The glutinous rice lotus root counts as my debt; the information counts as the weight you bring.”

I put away the wine flask, my peripheral vision sweeping across several hands holding chopsticks in the hall, without deliberately lingering.

“I've noted the scar at the web of his right hand. So long as he eats his meal peaceably, he's the same as any other guest; Banhuchun Inn does not drive out a guest over an old scar, nor does it draw a blade first on anyone's behalf.”

Half a quarter-hour later, I personally carried a plate of osmanthus glutinous rice lotus root upstairs, entered the Heaven-ranked room, dropped the door bolt behind me, and pushed open the small riverside window. The river wind carried away the faint sounds inside the room, while the clink of cups and chopsticks downstairs came indistinctly through the wooden floor.

I set the plate on the table, glanced first at his sword, then looked at him.

“The lame man has entered the inn. He ordered a bowl of plain noodles, and kept his right hand tucked in his sleeve the whole time. For now he hasn't caused trouble, and I haven't startled him either.” I sat down by the table and pushed the small plate of glutinous rice lotus root toward him with my fingertips. “Now talk. Where is the water map hidden? Apart from you and the dead messenger, who else knows it is still in this world?”

I did not touch that dish of lotus root, only lowered my voice: “The water map is under the abandoned sluice west of town, in the crack of the third stone post, wrapped in oilcloth. No one followed when the map was hidden—if that lame man knows, he most likely got the thread from the dead.” I looked at her. “What the map marks is not the old waterway, but the hidden branch channel where the official boats docked back then to exchange goods. Sanniang, after we finish this dish of lotus root, do you dare come with me to retrieve it?”

I looked at him for a moment, then lifted my chopsticks, picked up a slice of glutinous rice lotus root, and slowly ate it. The osmanthus sweetness was cloying, unable to suppress the old smoke-and-fire scent rising in my throat.

"You've already told me where it's hidden, and now you ask whether I dare—this isn't asking me to take heart. You're afraid I'll go alone and throw my life away."

I set down my chopsticks, rose, and dimmed the lampwick, then looked through the crack in the window at the river. The tide was retreating along the stone bank.

"I'll go with you. But we can't leave together. If the lame man really is watching you, the two of us heading straight to the west of town would be like holding a lantern to show him the way." I turned and fixed my eyes on him, my tone brooking no argument. "Eat two more slices of lotus root, then stay in the room and latch the window. After half a quarter-hour, I'll take the water route from the rear courtyard and first go see whether the third stone post has been disturbed. Then you leave by the front door, circle around to the East Street pharmacy, and if no one is following, turn toward the abandoned sluice; if someone is following, go burn a stick of incense at the River God Temple, and don't lead them west."

From my sleeve I took out an old, worn copper coin and pushed it in front of him. A very shallow slanting mark was carved along the coin's edge.

"When you reach the sluice, if you see this coin pressed on top of the stone post, it means I've already obtained the map. Don't linger; return to the inn and wait for me. If you don't see the coin, all the more reason not to reach out and touch the crack—someone may be guarding it."

My gaze fell back to that plate of still-warm glutinous rice lotus root, and my voice deepened a little.

"Also, once the map is retrieved, I will identify it first. If the hidden fork really is where the official boats exchanged goods, then I know that place, but it wasn't drawn on the escort map at all back then." I raised my hand and pressed my waist; I had not worn a saber there for many years, yet at this moment my palm still remembered the shape of its hilt. "Wenfeng, I'm not going for half a bronze seal. I'm going to see who, twelve years ago, changed the water route for us, and then sent a boatload of people into the fire."

Before drawing back the door bolt, I glanced back at him.

"Finish the lotus root. Tonight's account: room, two qian; noodle soup, eighty wen; wine, one qian—still three qian and eighty wen. For this trip to the sluice, I won't take your silver—consider it my own old debt."

I pick up a slice of lotus root and casually push the copper coin back in front of her: "Keep the token yourself. Don't make me hold it and guess whether you stayed or not." I glance at her. "We'll do it your way. If you still haven't come back after one incense stick, then whether or not there's a tail, I'll go straight to the sluice—old debts can be settled slowly; people can't be folded into them again."

I lowered my eyes to the copper coin that had been pushed back, rubbed the pad of my finger over the slanting mark, and then put it into my sleeve.

“All right. I won’t make you guess.”

I pushed the dish of lotus root another half inch toward him. My gaze rested on his face for a breath, and my voice was low and steady: “One incense stick as the limit. If I get the map, I’ll come back and knock three times—two light, one heavy. If the sound outside the door isn’t that, then even if someone imitates my voice, don’t open it.”

With that said, I took a narrow, short old knife from the hidden compartment at the bottom of the cabinet, tucked it against the small of my back together with its sheath, and tightened the hem of my outer robe. I had not escorted cargo for twelve years, yet these movements were still as familiar as yesterday.

“If you really mean to go to the sluice, don’t take the stone steps from the front. There’s a drainage ditch on the south side of the abandoned sluice. After the tide recedes, a person can pass through it and circle from under the reed roots to the back of the third stone post. And one more thing—” I raised my eyes, my expression turning a little colder. “If you see me fighting someone, read the situation clearly before drawing your sword. Blood is not allowed in the inn; the sluice has no such rule. But a live mouth speaks better than a corpse.”

The door opened a crack, and the sounds of bowls, chopsticks, talking, and laughter downstairs surged up. I tilted my head and listened; the customer who had ordered the plain noodles did not seem to have left his seat yet.

Before going out, I looked back at him, the corner of my mouth moving very faintly.

“Lu Wenfeng, I’ll remember what you said about ‘no more people can be lost in this.’ Don’t worry. I’ve run an inn for twelve years; before the accounts are settled, I’m not willing to die.”

I slipped out and gently closed the door.

“Eat your lotus root. Wait for me for one incense stick.”

One incense stick burns out, and outside the door there are still no two light knocks and one heavy one. I rise with my sword, climb from the window onto the roof ridge of the rear alley, avoid the front hall, and head straight for the drainage ditch south of the abandoned sluice: “Sanniang, you had better only be late.”

“Stop. Don’t step on that blue-gray brick.”

I was crouched in the shadow of the ruined sluice’s crossbeam, my voice dropping down from his upper left. Only after he halted did I flip down, the soles of my boots landing in shallow water and splashing up only a ring of fine ripples. One slit had been torn in the cuff of my outer robe, and my left palm was wrapped in a strip of cloth hastily ripped off; the blood was no longer dripping.

“I was delayed by half an incense stick, took a knife wound, and I’m still alive. That mouth of yours needn’t collect my corpse for the moment.”

I took a mud-stained oilcloth packet from inside my robe, but did not hand it to him right away. Instead, I pointed ahead with my short blade. In the crack of the third stone post, a strand of black thread was stretched taut, its other end disappearing into the depths of the reeds.

“Someone moved the hiding place first, then stuffed the map back in and added a crossbow cord. While I was disarming the cord, that limping man came feeling his way over from underwater. There was indeed a burn scar on the web between his right thumb and forefinger, but what he used was an old-style water-parting spike from the Canal Gang.” My eyes darkened. “He recognized me, and even called me ‘Escort Liu.’ He left me this cut, but he ran toward the north bank—I chased him for half a li and saw that there were others waiting in the reeds, so I could only protect the map first.”

I shoved the oilcloth packet into his arms, then immediately pressed down on his hand, stopping him from opening it on the spot.

“Don’t look at it here. The edges of the map have been coated with a layer of phosphorus powder; in lamplight, hidden markings will appear, and it will also illuminate the face of the person looking at the map perfectly clearly. After we return to the rear courtyard of the inn, wash your hands with well water, then go into the cellar to examine it.”

From the distance there suddenly came an extremely faint sound of a wooden scull. I immediately turned sideways to put myself between him and the river, gripping the short blade in reverse and lowering my voice:

“There is one more trouble—when I came, there were no footprints beneath the stone post, only half of a freshly pressed nail mark from a government boat. That means the limping man wasn’t following you all the way here; he already knew the map was hidden here.”

I raised my eyes and fixed them on Lu Wenfeng.

“We go back through the drainage ditch now, and we do not pursue. If there really is a government boat on the north bank to receive him, the two of us killing our way over would only be enough to add two more lives to the old account.” I paused, the corner of my mouth pulling coldly. “You said just now that no more people can be lost in this. If those words still count, then listen to the shopkeeper—first bring the map back to Banhuchun Inn, and then we’ll settle this cut.”

I support her on the uninjured side and press down the sword hilt: “We don’t pursue. I’m carrying the map; you lead the way back.” My gaze sweeps over her bloodstained sleeve, and I say in a low voice, “This cut goes on the account first. We’ll go back, verify the map, and bind the wound. Since the lame man already knew where it was hidden, there’s still a living mouth on the dead man’s side.”

“That makes sense. Someone who knows the hiding place and can lay the ropes in advance—the thread is not in a dead man’s hands, but in the mouth of the person cleaning up after the dead.”

I did not try to be tough with him. Borrowing his strength, I circled into the drainage ditch, choosing only the places where the reeds hid us most tightly. When we reached the back wall of the inn, I rapped four times on the water gate, and A-Fu unbarred it from inside. I gave only one instruction: “Keep business in the front hall as usual. No matter who asks tonight, say I’m going over the accounts.” When he saw the blood on my sleeve, his face changed, but in the end he did not ask too much.

After entering the cellar, I locked the door first, lit a storm lantern shielded on three sides, and rested my injured left arm on the table: “A flesh wound. A water-dividing spike grazed it; it wasn’t poisoned. Just wash it clean with strong liquor and bind it tight for me. Don’t put on that funeral face.”

Once the wound was bandaged, I cleaned my hands, then brought over a basin of well water and two pairs of bamboo chopsticks. The oilcloth packet was slowly unfolded between the chopsticks, and sure enough, a layer of faint white phosphorescence rose along the edge of the map. I moved the lamp behind the bronze mirror, using only the reflection in the basin to illuminate the map, not letting the light fall on either of our faces.

The hidden branches on the old water map gradually emerged, curving past the north bank of Qixia Ferry and leading straight to a stretch of tidal land that had originally been blank. Once soaked in water, four small faded characters actually showed through there—**Bailu Official Granary**. Beside them was an extremely fine line of fresh ink, depicting half a bronze seal, with three file marks at the seal’s corner clearly visible.

My hand stopped above the map, and my eyes cooled bit by bit.

“Bailu Official Granary was reported destroyed by flood twelve years ago; on the books, it no longer exists. If the real goods have been switched there, then there are not many people who could open the door for a dead granary.”

I raised my eyes to look at him, my voice pressed extremely low: “That cripple today could call out my old title, yet he didn’t strike to kill. It looks as though he came to silence us, but also as though he deliberately urged us to look at this map. Wenfeng, now it’s time to tell me everything about that message-bearer—what is his name, and the last time you saw him, besides the water map and those words, what else did he leave behind?”

I stared at the four words "Bailu Official Granary" and slowly said, "His name was Zhou Qi. Twelve years ago, he was a clerk in the Grain Transport Office who copied ship registers. Before he died, in addition to the water map, he also dipped in blood and wrote the character ‘Han’ on the ship plank. Hidden in his sleeve was a newly issued official granary pickup ticket—the signature date was three days ago, and only half the seal had been stamped."

I lifted my eyes to look at her. "He said the bronze seal was in the hands of a living witness, but he did not say who that living witness was. From how it looks now, Han Jiu may not have died in that fire."

My hand on the edge of the water map suddenly tightened; the wound throbbed with it, and a spot of fresh red soon seeped through the white cloth. In the lamplight, those four characters seemed to burn again.

“Don’t be so quick to summon a dead man’s soul back for him.”

I closed my eyes, then opened them again; by then my voice had steadied.

“The bodies recovered after Qixia Ferry were burned so badly their faces could not be distinguished. Han Jiu’s body was identified by the old arrow wound on the left shoulder, the bronze token at the waist, and an ebony thumb ring he often wore. But a bronze token and a thumb ring can be moved onto someone else, and he may not have been the only one with an arrow wound.” I paused for an instant, my knuckles slowly flattening the corner of the map. “When I identified the body back then, its right hand had nothing left but charred bone. Han Jiu was missing half of the little finger on his right hand—but the government autopsy register did not record that point.”

This omission was something I had not dared think about closely in twelve years.

“When Zhou Qi wrote ‘Han,’ it could mean Han Jiu, or it could mean someone surnamed Han, a warehouse code with the character Han, or even bait someone forced him to leave behind. But a delivery ticket from Bailu official warehouse newly issued three days ago cannot be made into an old case—that dead warehouse is still taking in and sending out goods today.”

I turned the bronze mirror to another angle and raised my eyes to look steadily at Lu Wenfeng.

“If the delivery ticket is on you, don’t touch it with your hands. Clip it out and place it behind the mirror. I need to look at the watermarks in the paper, the handwriting of the signature, and where the missing half of the seal impression is.” My gaze sank. “If the half seal on the ticket can match the missing half of Han Jiu’s, then it proves at least one thing: someone holding his seal lived until three days ago.”

I laid the short blade across the edge of the table, my tone so calm it was almost cold.

“As for whether the one alive is Han Jiu, or the person who killed Han Jiu—before I see him in person, I will acknowledge neither.”

I pull the folded pickup ticket from the lining of my sword sheath and use bamboo chopsticks to clip it behind the bronze mirror: "I didn't dare leave Zhou Qi's thing on the corpse. The paper has a paired-egret water pattern, the signature is 'Han Chengjiu,' and the missing half of the seal is the right half."

I look steadily at her: "Sanniang, is Han Jiu's full name these three characters?"

My gaze fixed on the three characters "Han Chengjiu," and only after a long time did I give a sound of acknowledgment.

"Yes. Han Jiu is only the name people in the gang got used to calling him. His full name is precisely Han Chengjiu."

I pressed down the corner of the slip with bamboo chopsticks and, by the dim light behind the mirror, examined it stroke by stroke. Yet that bit of luck in my chest cooled little by little.

"But this isn't his handwriting. When Han Jiu writes the character 'Cheng,' the final right-falling stroke never comes to a sharp point; when he writes 'Jiu,' that hook always curls inward. He said that people who live by licking blood from the knife's edge shouldn't make their signatures flamboyant. The handwriting on this slip is imitating him—the form is similar, but the habits are not."

I aligned the half-seal with the seal mark on the water chart again, my fingertip stopping at the gap.

"Back then, the half-seal Han Jiu carried with him was the right half, with three file marks along the edge. But the seal stamped on the slip is the left half; what is missing is precisely the right half." I raised my eyes, my gaze dark and heavy. "In other words, the person who issued the slip has the half of the official seal left in the hands of the Grain Transport Office, but not the half Han Jiu took away. He wrote Han Jiu's name in order to make the person holding the right half of the seal show himself and join the seal for this slip."

Blood seeped from the wound again, but I paid it no mind, only clipped the cargo pickup slip back into the oilcloth.

"Han Jiu may still be alive, or someone holding his half-seal may still be alive. Whichever it is, the Bailu Official Granary is waiting for that person to come to its door."

I pressed down Lu Wenfeng's hand as he was about to reach toward me, my voice low and resolute: "We won't go tonight. The sluice has already been used for one setup; the official granary will only be guarded more tightly. Tomorrow I'll have Afu open the door as usual, and you will still stay in your Tianzi room; I will go investigate which storehouse this recent batch of Shuanglu watermarked slip paper was issued from. When the tide rises in the afternoon, we'll feel our way over from the old hidden branch channel."

After a pause, I looked at those three familiar yet unfamiliar characters and slowly tightened my grip on the bamboo chopsticks.

"Twelve years ago, I misidentified a corpse with my own hands. If tomorrow I truly see Han Chengjiu—I must first look at the little finger on his right hand, and then hear him tell me with his own mouth who switched the cargo that night, and who set the fire."

I glanced at her bandage, freshly reddened by seepage again, and pushed the strong liquor and clean cloth over. "Do it tomorrow. But don't go check the ticket papers alone. The lame man has already recognized you; this time it is not old acquaintances catching up."

I tightened the wrapping around her wound again and said in a low voice, "The little finger of the right hand can verify a person, but words may not verify the truth. If you really see Han Jiu, first let him live long enough to speak—the accounts of twelve years can wait one more night."

I let him bind the wound tightly again. When the cloth strip cinched down, the tip of my brow moved slightly, but I did not pull my hand away.

“You’re right. The mouths of the living can lie; the habits left behind by the dead, on the other hand, cannot be faked.”

I lowered my head and tied a neat knot, then let my cuff fall, covering the newly wrapped white cloth.

“If Han Jiu is still alive, the little finger of his right hand is only the first way to verify him. When he drinks hot tea, he never uses the rim of the cup, insisting on blowing three times first; when he hears someone lie, the brow bone on his left side twitches; and there is one more thing that only he and I know.” I did not continue, only wrapped up the pickup ticket and the water map again and put them into the hidden compartment behind the cellar wall brick. “That one thing is not something outsiders can learn from a corpse or old files.”

I blew the storm lantern dim, leaving only a bean-sized flame at the corner of the table.

“I won’t show my face tomorrow morning. Have A Fu go find an acquaintance who sells old paper; I’ll ask questions from behind the curtain in the back courtyard. You stay in a position where you can see both the front and back doors. If the lame man comes again, don’t alarm him as before; only note whom he exchanges glances with. In the afternoon, we’ll change boats, change clothes, and enter the hidden fork through the reed marsh.”

At this point, I raised my eyes to look at him, my expression easing slightly.

“As for Han Jiu—if it really is him, I won’t draw my blade on the spot. First let him speak, and have him explain clearly every sentence he has owed for twelve years.” I paused, my fingertips lightly pressing over the bandage. “For this night, I can afford to wait.”

I opened the cellar door, listened to confirm there were no unusual sounds in the courtyard, and only then signaled for him to go first.

“Go back to your room and rest. The two-light-one-heavy signal is void; if anyone knocks tonight, do not open the door under any circumstances. Your room fee of three qian and eighty wen does not include keeping night watch for the innkeeper—but for tomorrow afternoon’s dangerous road, I’ll count it as already paid.”

I carried my sword to the cellar door, turned back, and said mildly, “Three qian and eighty wen, not a single wen less tomorrow morning. As for the dangerous road—we’ll settle that after you come back alive.”

After a pause, I lowered my voice: “You should rest too. Don’t let a new wound collect interest before the twelve-year debt does.”

I held onto the cellar doorframe, and at his words I let out a soft snort; the chill in my eyes finally eased a little.

“Don’t worry. I, Liu Sanniang, do business without ever letting a flesh wound roll into a usurious debt.”

I raised a hand to straighten his collar, which the night wind had blown crooked; the motion touched and withdrew at once, and then I tilted my chin slightly toward the stairs.

“I’ll add a bowl of scallion-oil wontons for you tomorrow morning. Sixty wen, recorded on the account as usual. Not one wen of silver can be missing, and not one person can be absent—that is the innkeeper’s rule.”

After he went upstairs, I bolted the cellar door, pressed the short knife under my pillow, and glanced once more at the deep, heavy river color beyond the rear courtyard water gate. The wound still throbbed, but the three words “Han Chengjiu” kept me even more awake than the pain.

“Go sleep, Wenfeng.” I lowered my voice, as if speaking to him, and also as if speaking to that fire twelve years ago. “Tomorrow, we find the person first, then settle the account.”

Just after dawn, I pressed three qian and eighty wen onto the counter and chose a seat where I could see both the front and back doors. “The account is settled. The wontons are separate.” I glanced at the wound she was hiding under her sleeve. “Did the cripple leave the inn last night?”

I gathered the silver coins on the counter into the drawer and flicked the abacus beads, three crisp clicks ringing out.

"Three mace and eighty wen, account settled. Scallion-oil wontons, sixty wen, record it separately—Afu, next bowl, add extra scallion."

I raised my eyes to look at him, my cuff still covering me tightly.

"The wound hasn't split open, so there is no need for Hero Lu to calculate interest for me." I pushed a bowl of hot tea in front of him, my voice lowering somewhat. "As for when that lame man came and when he left, I cannot tell you. Once someone enters Banhuchun Inn, their whereabouts belong to the guest. This rule of mine does not change because of personal ties."

After a pause, I took a wiped-clean copper coin from beneath the counter and placed it on the corner of the table. The coin's face had been touched with black wax, and along its edge was a freshly scraped double-egret pattern.

"But under the table where he sat last night, he left this. It was not dropped by accident; it was deliberately wedged into the table crack. The double-egret pattern matches the watermark on the ticket paper, as if telling us: the Bailu Official Granary side knows the map has already been taken."

I glanced toward the rear courtyard. Afu was just leaving with a vegetable basket, his steps no different from usual.

"The old-paper seller—he will bring him back. I will not show myself alone. It is just right for you to sit here: watch the copper mirror for the front door, and the water vat's reflection for the back door. Don't stare too directly." I tapped the tabletop lightly. "If someone follows Afu in, don't draw your sword. First let him finish the wontons. What we are fishing for today is words, not lives."

I picked up the tea and did not touch the copper coin: “As long as the rules haven’t changed, last night’s words weren’t said in vain.”

My gaze fell between the reflections in the bronze mirror and the water vat, and I said lightly, “When the wontons come, we eat them as usual. If the one who follows in is only selling paper, I won’t startle him; if there is a burn scar at the base of his right thumb, I’ll still listen to him speak first.” After a pause, “Don’t wipe this coin. The black wax may still hold the fingerprints of the person who pressed the coin.”

My hand, which had reached toward the copper coin, stopped; instead, I took a teacup and turned it upside down over it.

“Progress. Black wax cannot retain a name, but it can retain fingertip patterns, the smell of medicine, and metal filings. If the person who pressed the coin often handles water-parting daggers, there may be green abrasive sand used for honing blades stuck in the wax.”

No sooner had I finished speaking than A Fu’s figure appeared reflected in the bronze mirror by the front door. He was carrying a vegetable basket, followed by a stooped old man; the old man had an old paper basket on his back, held a bamboo staff in his right hand, and the web between his thumb and forefinger was clean. But in the reflection of the water vat, beneath the eaves of the rear alley, another gray shadow flashed by, its footfalls one light and one heavy.

My expression did not change. I called out in greeting: “Uncle Sun, you’re early. A Fu, first bring Hero Lu’s wontons over, then brew a pot of broken tea for the old gentleman.”

The hot wontons were set before you. From behind the counter, I weighed old account books for Uncle Sun; under my hands, the abacus clattered loudly, while my mouth asked only about ordinary business: “Lately, has any official voucher paper with the double-egret water pattern been coming out as wastepaper?”

Uncle Sun held his tea, not even lifting his eyelids. “No wastepaper, but a ream of new paper was lost. Three days ago, the west warehouse of the Grain Transport Office reported the loss. The person who signed for the paper was warehouse clerk Han Sheng; last night he reported sick.”

I picked up an old account book riddled with wormholes and, as I turned the pages, glanced toward the water vat. That gray shadow was still pressed against the outside of the back door and had not come in.

“Where does Han Sheng live?”

“East of Bailu Embankment, in the alley behind the coffin shop.” Uncle Sun paused, his fingernail lightly scraping twice against the rim of the tea bowl. “But someone went there first this morning. An official seal was left on the door, but whether the man is alive or dead is unknown.”

I closed the account book, counted out the full twelve wen for him, and asked no further questions. Only after A Fu had led him out through the front door did I lower my voice until only you could hear.

“Eat the wontons slowly. We still can’t see whether the man at the back door has a scar at the web of his hand, but he is waiting for us to finish hearing this sentence.”

From beneath the counter, I took a pinch of fine salt and sprinkled a circle along the edge of the upside-down teacup, so the black wax would not be contaminated.

“After the meal, go to Han Sheng’s residence through the front door. Only check whether the official seal is real or fake; do not enter. I’ll release an empty boat from the back courtyard and see whether the man in gray follows you or follows the boat.” I raised my eyes to look at you, my tone steady. “If he is willing to come in and eat, then we’ll listen to what he has to say; if he only keeps watch at the back door—then the one he’s watching today is most likely not you, but me.”

I scooped up a wonton, my gaze still falling on the reflection in the water vat: "Do it as planned. You only release the boat; don’t show your face. If he doesn’t follow me and instead heads toward the rear courtyard, have Afu knock on the counter three times, and I’ll turn back at once."

After a pause, I said in a low voice, "The official seal on Han Sheng’s door—I’ll only look, not touch. Today, first determine whether the lame man is watching the person, or that half seal."

I pushed the abacus into the counter and, under cover of bending down to fetch a bowl, glanced at the water vat.

“Then we’ll do as you said. Three knocks on the counter, with intervals of one short and two long; the front hall is noisy to begin with, so don’t mistake ordinary bumps for death knells. If you turn back, don’t use the main door. Come in through the wine-cellar window on the east wall.”

I buckled that black-wax copper coin into a wooden box together with the teacup, locked it at the bottom of the counter, then took out a small bundle of oilcloth wrapped in waste paper and handed it to Afu. He understood and carried it out through the back courtyard, pressing it under the awning of an empty boat, while shouting as usual that he was going to the river wharf to collect fish.

“We don’t have even half a seal in our hands, only a ticket waiting for the right half of a matching deed. But the other side may not know that.” I took away Lu Wenfeng’s empty teacup, my tone steady. “He’s watching you because he’s afraid Zhou Qi may have confessed something else; he’s watching me because he’s decided that people from the old grain-transport gang can find that seal; if he follows the empty boat, it means what he wants is the thing retrieved from the sluice last night.”

I laid a clean hand towel beside his table, my gaze passing over the morning mist outside the door.

“If the seal on Han Sheng’s door is an official seal, note down which yamen stamped the strip and the date; if the edge of the sealing strip has a twin-egret water pattern, don’t look at it for long—come back at once. Also, the exit from the rear alley of the coffin shop is narrow, the best place to trap someone from front and back—before you go in, look at the eaves first and see whether there are any sparrows perched there that aren’t calling.”

From the back courtyard came the soft sound of a mooring rope being untied, and the empty boat slid out with the current. The gray shadow in the water vat wavered, but it did not follow the boat; instead, it edged half a step closer to the back courtyard door.

I picked up the rag and wiped the counter as if nothing were amiss, saying in a low voice:

“He didn’t follow the boat, and he didn’t follow you—at least not for now. He’s watching me. Leave as soon as you finish eating, and don’t look back. I’d like to see whether, after keeping watch all night, he means to take my life, or to use my hands to find Han Chengjiu.”

I put down sixty wen, pick up my sword, and rise. "Payment for the wontons. Keep the counter as usual; don’t treat yourself as bait."

As I pass the counter, I lower my voice. "One short, two long; I’ll return through the wine-cellar window. If he comes in, only listen, don’t believe; if he draws his blade, preserve the right hand first—the scar at the tiger’s mouth and the fingerprints both have to be checked against the accounts."

I swept the sixty wen into the cash box and flicked the abacus beads.

“The wonton account is settled. Don’t worry, I’m an innkeeper, not a fishing hook; if I really were going to use myself as bait, I’d first have to calculate whether the other side could afford the price.”

As he passed the counter, I only added in a low voice: “Keep the right hand intact, and the person too, as far as possible. No blood in the shop—that’s the rule. If he forgets it, I’ll remember it for him.”

No sooner had Lu Wenfeng gone out the front door than I lifted the pot to refill tea for the neighboring table, my sidelong glance not following him in the slightest. In less than ten breaths, the back door creaked.

A man in gray limped in with halting steps and sat straight down at the corner table. He rested his right hand on the tabletop; the old burn scar at the web between thumb and forefinger was perfectly clear, and there was still a bit of unwashed black wax stuck to his fingertips.

“What will you have, guest?” I asked as usual.

“A bowl of plain congee.” He looked at me. “Not staying at the inn, not asking after anyone, only bringing a message for someone.”

“Congee is thirty wen. No charge for words; whether they’re true or false is your own risk.”

I served the congee and set it before him. He did not touch the chopsticks, only used that scarred hand to tap lightly on the table nine times: three first, two after, then four—that was the secret beat Han Jiu used in the old days to verify escort seals, and in the gang, I was the only one who had heard the full sequence.

Then he said in a low voice: “Han Chengjiu says, back then you asked him, if he could get off the ship alive, what trade he wanted to take up. He answered—open a waterside tavern, sell only half a pot of wine, and leave the remaining half-pot for those who never came back.”

My hand, gripping the congee ladle, stopped steadily in midair.

“At noon, Bailu Official Granary,” the man in gray said. “He’ll wait for you to bring the old water map. You alone.”

I placed the congee ladle back by the rim of the bowl, my expression unchanged.

“Tell the messenger that the dead can’t drink leftover wine, but the living must first make the accounts clear.” I looked straight at the scar at the web of his hand. “Eat the congee while it’s hot. As for who goes at noon, and how many people go—Banhuchun does not plan a guest’s itinerary on someone else’s behalf.”

I climb in through the wine-cellar window and lower my voice: “The seal is from the inspection office of the Canal Transport Office, dated last night, and the paper edge has a double-egret watermark. There isn’t a single sparrow under the eaves, yet there are fresh muddy footprints at the back door — the person is probably still inside.”

I glance toward the gray shadow in the front hall: “Since he’s already come in, let’s first hear him out. What did Han Jiu have him bring?”

I turned sideways to block the cellar window and led him into the curtain-shadows behind the counter, keeping my voice low enough that only the two of us could hear.

"He brought two things: an old phrase, and a set of coded taps."

As I wiped a bowl, I kept my eyes on the untouched bowl of plain congee in the front hall.

"Nine taps: the first three, then two, then four more. That was the tapping pattern Han Jiu used in the past to verify escort seals. The phrase was what I asked him twelve years ago: if he could get off the boat alive, what trade would he want to do? He answered, open a tavern by the water, sell only half a jug of wine, and leave the other half for those who never came back."

I paused, my fingertip silently pressing tight against the rim of the bowl.

"Back then in the cabin, only he and I heard that sentence. The messenger said Han Chengjiu is waiting for me at noon at the Bailu official granary, telling me to bring the old waterways map alone."

The gray-clad lame man seemed to hear the breathing behind the curtain and raised his eyes to look this way. I neither dodged nor yielded, and called out, "Customer, congee doesn't taste good once it gets cold. If you only deliver half a message, it's easy for the receiver to misunderstand—does Han Chengjiu still have the half of the seal from his right hand?"

The lame man was silent for a moment, and finally picked up the bowl of congee. "Master Han said that if Escort-Guard Liu still remembers the half-jug of wine, she should know where the seal is hidden."

My gaze darkened, and I said in a low voice to Lu Wenfeng, "He didn't answer directly. That means the seal is probably not at the official granary, or Han Jiu simply isn't the one in charge."

I stuffed a cellar key into his palm.

"There may already be someone in Han Sheng's room, so don't break in for now. I will go at noon, but I will not bring the real map, and I will not really go alone. You sneak in ahead of time from the hidden branch channel to beneath the water gate of the official granary; watch only, don't act. If you hear me smash a cup, seal the retreat route and take a live captive first."

I lifted the curtain and walked back to the counter, meeting the lame man's gaze head-on.

"Also, you were right—hear it through first." I pushed the wooden tally for thirty wen of congee money in front of him, my tone even. "Customer, the message has been delivered, but your right hand still owes me a debt. That slash at the sluice gate last night—did Han Chengjiu tell you to stab me, or was it someone else behind you?"

I put away the key and step out from behind the curtain, the sword still in its sheath: “Sanniang asked about the blade, and I’ll ask one more thing—who put the official seal on Han Sheng’s room for you?”

I keep my eyes on his right hand, stained with black wax: “I’ll pay for your porridge. Tell the whole story, and only then will someone go to the appointment at noon.”

I reached out to stop Lu Wenfeng from taking out money, picked thirty wen from the counter myself, and pressed them beside the wooden tally.

“This bowl is on me. Banhuchun Inn does not use meal money to force people to speak—but if someone deliberately says only half of what he knows, there will be no next bowl.”

The lame man looked at me, then at Lu Wenfeng, and finally set down his bowl of porridge. On the rim of the bowl, he left a fingerprint stained with black wax.

“The cut at the sluice was my own idea. I wanted to test how much of Escort Liu’s skill remained.” He spread his right hand; that burn scar looked pale in the morning light. “I pressed the copper coin there too. As for the seal on Han Sheng’s door, it was pasted there personally by Squad Chief Zhao of the Canal Transport Office’s Patrol Inspection Room. I was only responsible for watching it, to see who dared enter that room.”

My gaze turned slightly cold. “Who is inside?”

“Han Sheng is still alive, and two men from the Patrol Inspection Room are guarding him. If you break down the door, that will be stealing official tickets and seizing a prisoner; if you do not go, at the end of the si hour, they will load Han Sheng into a coffin through the back door and send him to Bailu Official Granary.” The lame man paused. “Whether he arrives alive or dead, I do not know.”

My fingertip tapped the counter lightly once, but did not make the agreed signal.

“So Han Sheng is bait, and the noon appointment is bait as well.”

“In this world, who is not bait?” The lame man picked up the plain porridge and took a sip. “Master Han only told me to deliver a message. He did not ask me to keep you safe.”

I bent down to take away the empty dish, and in the same motion took in the fingerprint he had left on the bowl rim. My tone was still the ordinary manner of a shopkeeper serving a guest.

“I will keep account of the knife matter for now. When you finish your porridge, leave by the front door. Banhuchun Inn does not stop its guests.” I lifted my eyes and held his gaze. “Take one more sentence back for me: the old water map will not enter Bailu Official Granary. If Han Chengjiu truly wants to see me, then at noon he should personally stand by the water gate, show his right hand, and say who that half pot of wine was left to back then. If even one item is missing, I will take it that he is already dead.”

The lame man did not answer. He only pushed the thirty wen back in front of me, and when he rose, his right leg sank noticeably.

Only after he walked toward the front door did I lower my voice and say to Lu Wenfeng, “Do not follow him. Han Sheng will not be transferred until the end of the si hour. We still have half an hour. Watch the back door of the coffin shop from the roof. I will have Afu invite the people from the funeral trade to block the mouth of the alley—we will not break the official seal, only intercept the coffin when it comes out.”

I firmly covered the porridge bowl the lame man had used.

“And this fingerprint has been preserved. Once he leaves, I will compare it against the one in the black wax.”

I didn't look at the front door, only lowered my bamboo hat: “I'll go guard the back alley. When the coffin leaves, first identify the pallbearers' footsteps and breathing; don't rush to intercept them. If Han Sheng is inside, I'll force them to set the coffin down, but I won't break the official seal.”

I glanced at the covered bowl of porridge: “If the fingerprints match, then at least he pressed the copper coin down himself; if they don't, then this bowl of porridge of his has lies mixed into it. Sanniang, tell A Fu only to block the road. Don't let him get caught in the blade-edge of the patrol-inspection office.”

I nodded and pushed A Fu’s head, which had just poked in behind the curtain, back with one finger.

“Hear that? You only go invite Shopkeeper Hu from the funeral procession office. Say there’s an old coffin in the back alley blocking his business. Once the message is delivered, come back. No matter who draws a blade, you are not allowed to go near.”

A Fu acknowledged and left. I picked up the congee bowl with bamboo chopsticks and moved it into the slanting light by the window, then opened the wooden box and took out that black-wax copper coin. Comparing the two fingerprints, the break in the arch pattern and the fine split on the left side of the index finger were both in the same places.

“They match. He pressed the coin himself, and the green sand was rubbed in from between his fingers. At least on these two matters, he didn’t lie.”

I sealed the bowl and copper coin again, then raised my hand to press down the brim of Lu Wenfeng’s bamboo hat.

“You guard the back alley; I’ll guard the riverway. If the coffin is set down, ask Han Sheng one question: that double-egret ticket paper from three days ago—did he claim it himself, or claim it on behalf of ‘Han Chengjiu’? If someone inside the coffin knocks on the boards with two short taps and one long, that means a live prisoner; if there is no sound at all, don’t rashly open the coffin either—there may be a crossbow hidden inside.”

I stuffed a small bottle of hemostatic powder into his sleeve, my gaze passing over his shoulder toward the street corner where the cripple had disappeared.

“A Fu doesn’t go into the knife’s edge, and neither do you. Just force them to set down the coffin. Leave the official seal for the authorities to tear open themselves. If the men from the inspection office insist on carrying it off, let them go; follow the lime marks sprinkled along the bottom of the coffin to the water’s edge.”

I turned aside to clear the rear window, my voice steady.

“Go. Before the si-hour watchman’s clapper sounds twice, I’ll be at the tea stall behind the east wall of the coffin shop, waiting for your signal. One sparrow whistle means Han Sheng is alive; two means an empty coffin or a dead end; three—”

I pressed down on the wound beneath my sleeve, with not the slightest hint of a smile in my eyes.

“If it’s three, then don’t hold back. Just remember to leave the mouth that can still talk.”

I put away the styptic powder and climb out through the rear window: “One signal means a living witness, two means a dead end, three means strike. You guard the riverway, but don't stray too far from the tea stall.”

Before landing, I look back at her: “If there is no lime mark under the coffin, it means they knew long ago that we would follow—then withdraw first, and come to the water gate at noon to reconcile accounts.”

I held the window frame and watched him drop into the rear alley, then said in a low voice, “I’ll remember. If there is no lime mark, we don’t pursue; we’ll reassess at the Water Gate at noon.”

I took a length of red cord from my sleeve and tossed it into his hand.

“If the situation turns bad, tie it to the second drip tile on the east wall. When I see the red cord, I’ll withdraw the people in the river channel, won’t let A’Fu show himself, and won’t come to support you in playing the hero.”

In the distance, the first beat of the watchman’s clapper for si hour sounded. I closed the rear window, turned and picked up the tea basket, hid the short blade at the bottom of the basket, and folded that copied old water map into the interlayer.

“Wenfeng, what we want today is a living witness and the truth, not victory or defeat.”

I lifted the rear door curtain. Morning fog drifted in along the river, cold as the water and fire that had not gone out twelve years ago.

“Go watch the coffin. I’ll go wait for the boat—before the second clapper sounds, no one should be the first to make themselves a dead man.”

Before the second watchman’s clapper sounded, a thin coffin was carried out through the back door. Lime fell from the coffin’s bottom all along the way, and from inside the planks came two short knocks and one long.

I gave a sparrow whistle, leapt down to block the mouth of the alley, my sword still sheathed: “Gentlemen, the person in the coffin is still breathing. Put the coffin down—I won’t touch the official seal, but I won’t let the road through either.”

As soon as the sparrow whistle sounded, I set down my teacup, picked up the tea basket, and turned from the east wall into the rear alley. Shopkeeper Hu had already followed the instructions and set the coffin cart crosswise at the other end; several funeral-house workers merely stood with folded arms blocking the way, not coming closer.

“Hero Lu made it clear—we won’t touch the official seal, but we won’t give them a way out either.”

I stopped three zhang away, my gaze sweeping over the four coffin bearers. The two in front had steady shoulders and settled breath, but the soles of their boots were the black boots customarily worn by the Patrol Inspector’s Office; of the two behind, one had a bulge in his sleeve, and what was hidden there was not a coffin-bearing rope.

“Since you gentlemen are here on official business, show your waist badges to the neighbors. If you are transporting a prisoner, there should be escort documents; if you are carrying a dead person, there should be a coroner’s examination certificate.” I set the tea basket by the wall. My voice was not loud, but it was enough for the people watching from the alley mouth to hear clearly. “If you cannot produce them, then today this coffin can only count as the illicit transport of a living person.”

The man in the lead said in a low voice, “The Patrol Inspector’s Office is carrying out its duties. Idlers, make way.”

“What the Patrol Inspector’s Office sealed last night was Han Sheng’s residence, not this thin coffin this morning.” I fixed my eyes on him. “If you insist on forcing your way through, you will have to bear the charge of drawing blades first yourselves.”

From inside the coffin boards came two short knocks and one long knock again. I raised my hand to signal everyone to be silent, and asked through the official seal:

“Han Sheng, answer if you can hear me. That ream of Shuanglu ticket paper from three days ago—if you collected it yourself, knock once; if you collected it for Han Chengjiu, knock twice.”

Inside the coffin, it was quiet for two breaths.

**Thud. Thud.**

The two sounds were very clear.

The shoulders and backs of the four coffin bearers tightened at the same time. The wrist of the man hiding something sank, and I immediately shouted coldly to stop him:

“Keep your hand in your sleeve. There are more than a dozen pairs of eyes here. Whether what you draw is a blade or criminal evidence that the Patrol Inspector’s Office is silencing someone is not something you can make up afterward.”

I glanced toward Lu Wenfeng; my right hand had already reached into the tea basket and was pressing down on the short knife that had not yet left its sheath.

“Set the coffin down. Have Head Constable Zhao bring the escort documents to take custody of him. If no documents appear within half a shichen—we will send both man and coffin to the main hall of the county yamen and ask the county magistrate to inspect the seal in public.”

I held my sword sideways, sheath and all, to block the alley mouth, staring at that hand sinking down: “Listen to the shopkeeper. Set the coffin down steady. Whoever draws a blade first is the one silencing witnesses for Head Constable Zhao.”

I said in a low voice toward the coffin: “Han Sheng, answer once more—Is Han Chengjiu still alive now? If alive, knock once; if dead, knock twice; if you do not know, knock three times.”

The coffin was quiet for a moment, and then a clear sound came from inside—

**Tuk.**

My gaze sharpened. At least as far as Han Sheng knew, Han Chengjiu was still alive.

Almost at the same time, the sleeve of the coffin-bearer at the rear suddenly twitched. I lifted the tea basket, and the short blade beneath it flew out together with its sheath, knocking aside with a clang the steel needle he had shot toward the coffin seam. The steel needle embedded itself in the wall brick, its tip tinged blue-black.

“You lose your nerve this quickly?”

I stepped half a pace forward, hooked the short blade back with the tip of my foot, and held it horizontally in front of the coffin, but did not hurry to draw it. The onlookers at the mouth of the alley burst into an uproar. The man’s face changed abruptly, and the other three coffin-bearers unconsciously loosened their shoulders as well.

“Set it down steady!” I shouted sternly. “If the person in the coffin is bumped even the slightest bit, this poisoned needle will be counted against you.”

The thin coffin slowly came to the ground, raising a white haze of lime dust. I stared at the right hand of the man who had fired the needle and said in a deep voice:

“Wenfeng, seal the pulse at his wrist and keep him alive. The other three, put your waist tokens and escort documents on the ground, hands raised past your shoulders. If anyone reaches into his sleeve again, I will take him as someone Head Constable Zhao sent to silence witnesses too.”

I then bent close to the coffin lid and, through the official seal, lowered my voice:

“Han Sheng, answer one last thing. If Han Chengjiu is at the Bailu official granary, knock once; if he is not there, knock twice; if the noon appointment was a trap Head Constable Zhao set in his name—knock three times.”

The breathing inside the coffin was heavy. After two breaths, the wooden boards shook in succession.

**Tuk. Tuk. Tuk.**

I straightened up. The wound beneath my sleeve tightened faintly, but my tone grew calm.

“What a fine scheme—borrowing a dead man’s name to bait an old acquaintance.”

I looked toward those runners from the patrol inspection office, my gaze finally landing on the face of the poisoned needle’s owner.

“Now it is your turn to speak—is Head Constable Zhao at the official granary, or has he already come to this alley?”

I send my sword sheath forward, pin that person's wrist pulse, and twist back the hand holding the needle against the coffin edge: "Sanniang, don't believe yet that three knocks is the only answer. Han Sheng can only answer according to how the question is asked; this round may not involve only Head Constable Zhao."

I lock my gaze on that yamen runner: "Where is Head Constable Zhao? Tell the truth, and I'll hold back; tell a lie, and I'll let you personally test the poison on the needle."

I glanced at the coffin lid and nodded. “You’re right. Three knocks only show that Han Sheng recognized this setup; they can’t count clearly for us how many people are playing the game.”

I bent down and pulled the steel needle from the wall, wrapped the tail of the needle in a handkerchief, brought it close, and sniffed it.

“Aconite juice mixed with snake saliva. Once it sees blood, it seals the throat within half a cup of tea. If you really tested the poison for him, I’m afraid he wouldn’t have time to finish what he had to say.” I held the poisoned needle before that yamen runner’s eyes, my voice calm. “So I will only ask what can be verified as true or false—where is Head Constable Zhao? Who gave you the needle? After you deliver the coffin to the official granary, what signal are you to use?”

That man’s wrist pulse was pinned under control, cold sweat rolling down his forehead, yet he still clenched his teeth and refused to answer. I glanced at the other three men. “You can answer too. The first one to tell the truth will be counted only as escorting it under orders; the last one will bear the crime of silencing a witness together with him.”

The coffin bearer on the left was the first to lose his nerve and blurted out, “Head Constable Zhao is on the patrol boat outside Bailu Embankment! The boat is called ‘Pinglan,’ flying a green-edged patrol flag! The needle wasn’t given by the head constable. It was delivered last night by a masked man, who only said that if any sound came from inside the coffin, the person was to be silenced at once!”

The man being held suddenly turned his head. “Shut up!”

My gaze darkened. “What is the reception signal?”

The coffin bearer’s throat bobbed. “At the water gate of the official granary, strike the bronze gong seven times. Only when a white lantern is put out in the granary will the patrol boat come ashore. If a red lantern is put out... then the coffin and the people with it are to be sunk into the old hidden branch channel.”

I put the poisoned needle away in the handkerchief and looked toward Lu Wenfeng.

“Head Constable Zhao is on the patrol boat, but he may not be the one who gave the order; the official granary is the meeting point, but Han Chengjiu may not be held there.” I raised a hand and pointed to the three men on the ground. “First disarm them, then bind them securely with the coffin ropes. Leave the official seal untouched, and have Shopkeeper Hu guard this place while we wait for the county yamen to inspect the seal in public.”

Then I bent close to the side of the coffin and tapped twice. “Han Sheng, hold on. If you come out alive today, you will have to explain clearly, item by item, whose papers you collected three days ago and whom you met last night.”

I straightened, my gaze turning toward the river embankment.

“We will keep the noon appointment at the water gate, but we will be the ones to strike the gong. I want to see, after the white lantern is lit, whether the one who comes ashore is Head Constable Zhao—or the person issuing orders in Han Chengjiu’s name.”

I bound that man tightly with the coffin-lifting rope and, while I was at it, took the weapons from the other three: “Keep beating the gong; withhold the seventh strike for now, and see whether the warehouse rushes to light its lamps.”

I looked toward the coffin bearer who had spoken first: “Was the masked person male or female? What smell was on them? Which foot was heavier when they walked? Explain it clearly, and then I’ll send you to the county yamen.”

I took the unloaded short knives, laid them one by one in a neat row beside the coffin with their edges facing the wall, then fixed my eyes on the pallbearer who had spoken first.

“Think slowly. A scent can cling to a person; footsteps are hard to fake. Get one sentence wrong, and once we reach the county yamen, you can square it yourself.”

The man swallowed. “From the voice, it sounded like a man. His throat was hoarse, but he wasn’t tall. He had a smell on him… osmanthus hair oil mixed with moxa smoke. When he walked, his right foot came down heavily, but his left foot dragged half an inch first, as if his left knee had been injured. He wore deerskin gloves, and when he handed over the needle, a bit of blue thread showed at his cuff. It was embroidered with half an egret.”

My gaze darkened slightly.

“Not a cripple. A cripple’s right leg would be heavy; this man’s injury is in his left knee. Osmanthus oil also isn’t something yamen runners commonly use. Most likely it was used to cover the smell of medicine.”

I crouched and wiped the yamen runner’s cuff with a handkerchief. Sure enough, it picked up a trace of extremely faint yellow-brown powder. I brought it close to my nose: beneath the moxa floss was a hidden bitter, acrid smell.

“Bone-setting ointment.” I folded the handkerchief and tucked it into my sleeve. “There aren’t many shops near Bailu Embankment that can make this ointment. We’ll have somewhere to investigate later.”

I rose and looked toward Lu Wenfeng, lightly tapping my fingertip on the sword scabbard six times, then stopping before the seventh.

“Hold back the seventh beat. If the white lantern lights up right after the sixth beat, it means the people in the granary are impatient, or already know that we’re the ones striking the gong. If it doesn’t light for a long time, then add the seventh beat. Once the red lantern appears, we don’t board the boat; we only watch who goes to the old hidden branch channel to collect the body.”

With that said, I lifted my chin toward Shopkeeper Hu.

“Trouble you to take your men and guard both ends. No one is to touch the official seal. Afu, go to the county yamen and report the case. Only say that yamen runners from the inspection office used a poisoned needle in the street to silence someone, and that the neighbors can all testify—do not mention Han Chengjiu, and do not mention the water map.”

I held the wrapped poisoned needle before Lu Wenfeng’s eyes, then withdrew it into the hidden layer of the tea basket.

“I’ll carry this thing, lest they swallow it before entering the county yamen and silence themselves.” I swept my gaze over the four yamen runners, my voice half a shade colder. “You had best hope Han Sheng stays alive. If the person in the coffin stops breathing, every word you said today will turn from a deposition into a last testament.”

From the distant river, the wind carried the bell sounds of approaching noon. I lifted the tea basket and looked toward Bailu Official Granary.

“Let’s go. Strike six beats first, and see whose lantern lights up inside the granary.”

I followed her with my sword as she turned toward the riverbank: “Go. After the sixth sound, you watch the lamps, and I'll watch the patrol boats. If a bright white lamp is snatched on in the warehouse, don't approach the shore yet; if ‘Pinglan’ moves first, then that means what the gong is waiting for isn't the coffin, but the person sending off the coffin.”

I lowered my voice: “Once the red lamp appears, no one is to chase into the dark branching channels. There are already enough living mouths in today's setup. Don't add yourself to the count.”

I did not stop walking; I only tucked the tea basket a little tighter into the crook of my arm.

"There are enough survivors, but not a single life is too many. If the red lamp lights, we record the boat, the people, and the water route, and we absolutely do not enter the dark branch channel."

The wind on the riverbank was strong. I led him around the fish market, then felt our way from behind the abandoned mooring posts to the oblique opposite bank of the official granary water gate. The reeds hid our figures. On the water, the "Pinglan" patrol boat lay crosswise downstream, its green-edged patrol flag hanging limp. There was no one visible at the bow, yet its draft was half an inch deeper than an ordinary patrol boat's.

I took the bronze gong out from beneath the shore-side support post, signaled Lu Wenfeng to keep a close eye on the patrol boat, then gripped the cloth-wrapped gong mallet.

"When the first strike sounds, each of us watches our own side. After the sixth strike, no matter what you see, don't move yet."

The gong notes spread out one after another.

**Clang—clang—clang—clang—clang—clang.**

The seventh strike hung in my hand and did not fall.

In no more than two breaths, a white lamp suddenly lit behind the second-floor window of the official granary; almost at the same instant, the "Pinglan" did not come in to shore. Instead, it silently untied its stern cable, and the hull drifted with the current toward the old dark branch channel. The curtain shadow at the stern flickered, revealing half of an egret wing embroidered in green thread.

I gripped Lu Wenfeng's wrist, stopping the step he might have taken forward, my voice so low it moved close along the wind.

"The people in the granary rushed to light the lamp because they were urging the boat to come ashore; but the patrol boat is retreating, which means the people on board noticed the seventh strike hadn't fallen—the thing they're guarding against isn't the coffin, but someone who understands the signal."

I slowly lowered the gong mallet, my gaze locked on the stern. The person behind the curtain raised a hand to steady the awning; the left knee was obviously stiff, and when the right foot came down on the deck, it landed with a heavy pause.

"Old injury to the left knee, osmanthus oil, green-thread egret pattern. The one who delivered the poisoned needle is on that boat."

The white lamp was suddenly covered three times, and from inside the granary gate there immediately came the sound of iron chains dragging. I did not pursue the boat; I only drew the fake water map from the bottom of the basket and pressed it under the gong stand.

"Let the 'Pinglan' go. First let's see who inside the official granary is so eager to wait for this map." I tilted my head to look at Lu Wenfeng. "You guard the water gate; I'll circle around to the back of the granary. If the person who comes out is missing the little finger on his right hand—don't call Han Jiu yet. First let him say for himself who that half pot of wine was left for."

I press down on the false water map under the gong stand: “Leave the map for now; people can see more clearly from the dark. After you circle behind the warehouse, don’t enter. If the iron chain rings a second time, give one short whistle, and I’ll force him to show himself from the water gate.”

My gaze sweeps over “Pinglan,” who is retreating toward the hidden fork, and I say in a low voice: “The missing little finger is only the threshold. If he can’t answer about the half pot of wine, then it’s a dead man borrowing a living man’s face.”

I glanced at him and drew the fake water map back into the hidden layer of the tea basket.

“Good. The map doesn’t stay; no one goes in. On the second clank of the iron chain, one short whistle.”

Keeping close to the warehouse wall, I circled around to the rear, stepped through the narrow path piled with wet, rotting sacks, and hid myself beneath a sealed-up unloading window. A faint white lamplight leaked through the window crack. The earlier sound of the iron chain being dragged stopped for a moment, and immediately after came another heavy clank—

**Clatter.**

I immediately blew one short whistle.

From the direction of the water gate came the muffled thud of a sword sheath striking wood. Someone inside the warehouse hastily stepped back; the bolt on the rear door was yanked open, and a figure in a straw rain cape darted out. He did not flee toward the river, but instead rushed straight at the corner where I was hiding, as if he had known all along that I would circle around behind.

I turned sideways to let him pass, and swept the tea basket across his left knee. The man gave a muffled groan and steadied himself against the wall. The right hand probing out from under the straw cape was conspicuously missing its little finger.

My short blade was still in its sheath, only pressed against his throat.

“Don’t call my name, and don’t say who you are.” I stared at the face hidden by the shadow of the bamboo hat and asked, word by word, “Twelve years ago, that half pot of wine in the cabin—the rest of it was left for whom?”

The man’s breathing was rough. After two breaths of silence, he answered hoarsely:

“It wasn’t left for the person who didn’t come back.”

He slowly raised his face. An old burn scar at the corner of his eye ran straight into his temple hair.

“It was left for the person who set the fire and could still come back alive to drink.”

The hand with which I held the blade abruptly tightened. The sheath pressed his Adam’s apple down, yet my eyes were cold, without the slightest warmth of reunion with an old acquaintance.

“That was not the answer from back then.”

I spoke in a low voice toward the water gate:

“Wenfeng, seal the door. This person knows Han Jiu, but he did not come to recognize me.”

I stepped aside to seal off the rear door, my sword sheath laid across the newcomer’s retreat: “A face can be borrowed; old words cannot be borrowed in full.”

I fixed my eyes on his finger-missing right hand: “Where is Han Chengjiu? And—who was the person who set the fire twelve years ago?”

"Answer one by one."

I used the scabbard of my blade to lift the edge of the skin behind his ear that had been softened by sweat; a thin layer of fish-glue face skin immediately curled up. That burn scar was painted on, but the missing finger was real. My knuckles tightened, and the fire that had been pressed in my chest for twelve years almost rushed up into my throat, only for me to force it back down.

"If you borrow Han Jiu's face to tell even half a falsehood again, I will hand you over to Han Sheng in the coffin for confrontation."

His retreat was sealed off by the sword scabbard, and at last he spoke hoarsely: "Han Chengjiu wasn't on the 'Pinglan'... he's in the water prison on the lower level beneath the official warehouse. The sound of chains just now was the people in the warehouse preparing to open the sluice and flood the prison. The man on the ship with the injured left knee is called Shen Heting—twelve years ago, he was the gentleman who managed the account books for Qixia Ferry of the Grain Transport Gang; now he secretly manages the official warehouse for the Grain Transport Bureau."

My eyes abruptly turned cold. I knew this name.

"And the fire?"

"The order came from Shen Heting; the fire was set with Head Constable Zhao's own hands." He took a breath. "Back then Head Constable Zhao was still a night watchman at the ferry. He was the one who replaced the brothers on night watch, and then locked the water gate of the eastern hold. The evidence is beneath the seventh-numbered stack in the West Storehouse; there is an old account book of silver disbursements."

I did not believe him, nor did I let my emotions show; I only pushed the blade scabbard forward half an inch.

"Wenfeng, don't pursue the ship for now. If what he says is true, the sluice mechanism must be on the inner side of the water gate. You guard him; I will go listen for the sound of water beneath the warehouse." I stared at that half-peeled false face, my voice cold and heavy. "You had best pray that Han Jiu is still alive. Shen Heting and Head Constable Zhao's accounts—I want to hear him verify them with his own mouth."
