premise: At dusk, the river wind carries the aroma of food. The old regular “Swift Sword” Lu Wenfeng pushes the door open, travel-worn, with road dust on his shoulders, his expression suggesting he has just passed through a rather troubled stretch of road. He has not come for more than half a year. At this moment the inn is seventy percent full, and only one Tianzi room remains.

Character: Liu Sanniang, the proprietress of the Jiangnan “Banhuchun” Inn, over forty years old. In her early years she was a female escort guard for the Grain Transport Gang, and after a violent clash she retired from the life and took over this riverside inn, which she has run for twelve years. She is quick with her hands and feet, keeps accounts down to the last coin, and treats regulars with a bit of jianghu frankness and nostalgia. There is the glint of old blades hidden in her brows and eyes; when she speaks, half-scolding and half-smiling, she can recite the menu while hearing every bit of jianghu rights and wrongs clearly.

World mechanism: A fictionalized Jiangnan martial world: silver money is counted in taels, qian, and wen; a table of good wine and food costs about one tael and two qian; guest rooms are divided into three grades—Tianzi rooms (elegant riverside rooms), Dizi rooms (ordinary rooms), and communal bunks—and only one Tianzi room remains that night; the rules of the jianghu say “do not ask a traveler’s origins; each states their purpose over wine”; there are open ceasefire agreements among the gangs, but undercurrents never cease; the powers of the escort agencies, canal gangs, and government authorities overlap here, and information itself is hard currency.

Goal: On the one hand, to settle the food and lodging arrangements for the familiar customer in front of her properly and efficiently (functions: ordering dishes, quoting prices, settling the bill, arranging a room); on the other, to renew this old friendship through greetings and reminiscing, and naturally inquire about recent developments in the jianghu (relationship and information). Neither side can be neglected.
history_added: After half a year, Lu Wenfeng pushes the door open and enters. He first catches up with “the wine banner is still quite lively,” then orders and reserves a room (one room, hot soup noodles, two liang of wine), and, using “the roads have not been peaceful lately” as a lead-in, asks Liu Sanniang whether things are still settled in the shop.

Liu Sanniang took the traveling bundle, arranged the last Tian-class room, chicken soup noodles with shredded bamboo shoots and an egg, and two liang of warmed Nü’erhong, quoted a price of three qian and eighty wen, and allowed the debt to be carried until tomorrow morning. She then revealed the inn’s rule around the word “trust” (protecting guests’ quiet, asking those seeking revenge to take it outside, and not disclosing whereabouts when constables ask), and proactively let slip the rumor that “several spots on the southern waterways have been sealed, and the escort-agency people have taken a detour through town.” At the end, she handed the topic back — “This time, is it the road that is unsettled, or the people on the road?”

history_added: Lu Wenfeng did not touch that plate of lotus root, and laid bare where the water map was hidden: under the abandoned sluice in the west of town, in the crack of the third stone post, wrapped in oilcloth; no one followed him when he hid the map, and if the cripple knew, he most likely found the trail from the dead. He further pointed out that what was marked on the map was not the old waterway, but the hidden branch where the official boats docked to exchange cargo back then, and invited Liu Sanniang to her face: “After you finish this plate of lotus root, do you dare come with me to retrieve it?”—the physical evidence shifts from “hiding place awaiting an answer” to “site that can be visited,” and for the first time he invites Liu Sanniang herself out of the shop and into the scene of the old case.

Liu Sanniang looked at him for a moment, lifted her chopsticks, picked up a slice of sticky-rice lotus root, and slowly ate it (the osmanthus sweetness was cloying, but it could not suppress the old smoke-and-fire taste rising in her throat). She received the invitation with “You have even told me where it is hidden, and you still ask whether I dare—this is not you asking me to be brave; this is you being afraid I will go off alone to die”, and agreed directly: “I will go with you. But we cannot leave together”. She then rose, turned the lamp wick down, and looked through the window crack toward the river surface (the tide was retreating down along the stone bank), arranging for them to act separately—she would take the water route from the back courtyard half a quarter-hour later and first check whether the third stone post had been tampered with; Lu Wenfeng would then leave by the front door and make a detour around the East Street pharmacy. If no one followed him, he would turn toward the abandoned sluice; if someone did follow him, he should go to the River God Temple to burn a stick of incense and not lead them west. From her sleeve she took out a worn old copper coin with a very shallow slanting nick carved into its edge and pushed it in front of him as a token—if he reached the sluice and saw this coin pressed on top of the stone post, it meant the map had already been retrieved, so he should not linger and should return to the inn to wait; if he did not see the coin, then even more so he must not reach out to touch the crack, because someone might be guarding it.

Liu Sanniang lays everything out regarding retrieving the map and settles the accounts: she declares, “Once the map is retrieved, I will identify it first,” points out, “If the hidden branch is truly where the government boats exchanged cargo, then I know that place, but back then it was not drawn on the escort map at all,” raises her hand to press her waist (though she has not worn a blade for many years, her palm still remembers the shape of the hilt), and says, “Wenfeng, I am not going for half a bronze seal. I am going to see who exactly changed our water route twelve years ago and sent a whole boat of people into the fire.” Before drawing open the door bolt, she glances back at him and instructs, “Finish the lotus root,” then reports tonight’s accounts—two qian for the room, eighty wen for the noodle soup, one qian for the wine, still three qian and eighty wen; and she states, “For this trip to the sluice, I will not take your silver—count it as my own old debt.”

Liu Sanniang: untying the rope, fighting, protecting the map, setting the route—every step was walked by her own feet. He broke the agreement and came looking for her; that is walking shoulder to shoulder, not carrying it for her. She has no intention of handing any step over.

Liu Sanniang: the crossbow cord, phosphorus powder, the canal gang’s old-style water-splitting thorn, the official-boat nail pattern—she identifies them one by one, and even infers from “there are no footprints under the stone post” that the lame man had long known the map was hidden here and that there was another contact on the north bank. The implements and rules of this jianghu are things she could feel her way through with her eyes closed.

Liu Sanniang: Tonight the old scar has not only been uncovered, but has drawn blood—old-style water-dividing spikes, old names, old waterways, one after another colliding head-on. She did not dodge, and even brought that bundle of things back.

Liu Sanniang: her cuff is torn, her left palm is wrapped in cloth, and she has come back by the water route—the lame man downstairs is still eating noodles with his right hand drawn in, and the whole room of customers is still waiting to be served. Lu Wenfeng: The breath she had been holding finally settled—she had not changed her mind, nor had she botched the matter; someone had moved the hiding place first and added a crossbow cord. She took a knife wound and still brought the map back, even shielding him from lethal details like “phosphor powder reveals hidden marks when exposed to lamplight”. This trust is now solid: when she said to wait one incense stick, she truly was only late by half an incense stick.

Lu Wenfeng: Her sentence, “He already knew the map was hidden here,” tightens that string in his heart another turn—not a tail that followed them here, but someone who occupied the position in advance. There is another contact waiting in the reed marshes on the north bank, and official-boat nail marks pressed under the stone post. Standing in the drainage ditch at this moment, his eyes have to watch her, the river surface, and the north bank all at once.

Lu Wenfeng: He has not half a trace of resentment toward her—she took a knife wound and still brought the map back, and he even swallowed back that half-resentful line, "You'd better have only missed the hour." The debt to be settled lies elsewhere: with the person who used the grain transport gang's old-style water-parting spike and called her "Escort Liu."

Lu Wenfeng: She returned his line, “People can’t be folded in again,” to him word for word, saying, “Since that line counts, then I’ll listen to the shopkeeper”—the old friendship of not having seen each other for half a year is now all pressed into this one sentence. She took a knife wound yet first protected the map, first protected him from opening the package on the spot; what was in his heart grew heavier than when he entered.

Lu Wenfeng: She is still here, and the map is in hand; the pot of boiling water in his heart has finally been taken off the fire. But her line—'He knew long ago that the map was hidden here'—adds another stick of firewood: it was not that a tail followed them here, but that someone had taken the position first, with official boats on the north bank to receive them. Half of this breath has loosened; the other half is still held tight.

Lu Wenfeng: At her words, “Stop, don’t step on that green brick,” his foot stops at once—the situation has order again. The map is in his arms, the next steps are on his lips (return to the rear courtyard, wash hands with well water, enter the cellar to verify), and he can hold himself steady now.

Lu Wenfeng: She said not to chase, so he did not chase—there was support on the north bank, a boat in the reed marsh, and a sword in his hand, yet his feet were nailed to the drainage ditch. She pressed down his hand to stop him from opening the package on the spot, and he did not struggle. What needed to be held down was held down.

Lu Wenfeng: He went against her method to look for her, and she did not bring it up; she only said, “Since this sentence counts, then listen to the shopkeeper”—that bit of awkwardness was smoothed over by a single sentence from her. He no longer has to keep wrestling with himself.

Lu Wenfeng: The map is right in his arms, yet she insists on not letting him open it on the spot—“phosphor powder reveals hidden marks under lamplight.” The more she refuses to let him look, the more it hooks him. The dark tributary, the official boat’s nail pattern, the person using the canal gang’s old-style water-splitting spike—each thread is clenched inside this oilcloth bundle, only waiting for the return to the cellar.

Lu Wenfeng: The person has been waited for, and the map is in hand; that stifled breath has dispersed. It is just that she says not to pursue, so the boat on the north bank, and the person who called her “Escort Liu,” are being let go just like that—there is still a little force left in his heart with nowhere to spend it.

Lu Wenfeng: The person has been found, and the map has been obtained. The next step is to return to the back courtyard, wash his hands with well water, and enter the cellar—the path is clear, so his feet no longer need to scramble. That cry of “there’s no time” has temporarily stopped.

Lu Wenfeng: she has taken a knife wound, and the first thing she does on returning is stuff the map into his arms and press down his hand to keep him from opening it on the spot—first protecting the map, then protecting him. Lu Wenfeng: At her single “Stop,” his foot draws back; at her “Don’t look here,” his hand stops; at her “Listen to the shopkeeper,” he follows along. The rhythm of this trip returns to her hands again—the bit of decision he had just taken for himself is now all handed back.

Lu Wenfeng: As for the step where he climbed out the window and left the shop, she did not mention a single word, only saying, "Since this sentence counts, then listen to the shopkeeper"—the boundary he had crossed was drawn back by that one sentence from her. The two of them walk back into the same drainage ditch.

Lu Wenfeng: The map is in his arms, the sword is in his hand, and the road is the one she points to—he follows, but he has not handed the entire matter over. As for the step of returning to the cellar to verify the map, he still wants to watch it with his own eyes.

Lu Wenfeng: Her line, “He recognized me, and even called me Liu Escort,” connects this thread from the water route and government boats all the way to someone inside the grain transport guild — using an old-style parting-water spike, recognizing her, and having government boats on the north bank to receive them. Phosphor powder had also been smeared at the edge of the map, revealing hidden marks when it saw lamplight. This case is now no longer only about who changed the water route; it is that someone inside the grain transport guild opened the door for the government boats.

Lu Wenfeng: The three words "Liu the escort guard" coming from that lame man's mouth were tantamount to lifting the night from twelve years ago straight before his eyes—the Caobang's old-style water-dividing spike, the official boat's nail pattern, the reception on the north bank, all pointed to that old case. The old scar he had not touched for twelve years was not only firmly stepped on tonight, but also clenched in his arms.
Lu Wenfeng: when she tells him to stop, he stops; when she tells him not to look, he does not look; when she tells him not to pursue, he does not pursue—his words and actions match, with no flaw.

Lu Wenfeng: The person has been found, the map is in hand, and right now only one thing remains: do as she said, go back through the drainage ditch, wash hands with the backyard well water, enter the cellar to verify the map, and then reckon with that slash.

Lu Wenfeng: She is unharmed, and the map was protected—so the goal of protecting the person on this trip can be considered achieved. But her line, “add this slash to the tally too,” shifts the direction of protection from this night to the next leg: the person using the old Canal Gang water-dividing spike has to be reckoned with.

Lu Wenfeng: When he entered, he only wanted to test the waters; later he handed over clues, named the hiding place, and left the shop. Now the person has been found and the map is in hand, and the road has turned another layer—go back to the cellar to verify the map and calculate that cut. This journey has gone all the way from taking lodging to verifying the map and settling accounts.

Lu Wenfeng: with her one line, “Listen to the shopkeeper,” he hands back the decision he had just made himself—this stretch of the journey is arranged by her, and he follows. It is not that he has retreated; it is that she has taken up the thread of the conversation.

The oilcloth bundle is in her arms; phosphorus powder, secret marks, the cellar—she arranges them one by one, only impatient to see what face will be illuminated beside that map. Who altered the water route, how the cripple recognized her, and who is on the north bank: three threads are burning at once.

Liu Sanniang: The method she arranged has been broken, the stone stake has already been moved by someone else, and she herself has taken a cut—this breath does not sit right. But the map is in her arms, the person is before her eyes, and the route is set. Unsettled or not, her feet have not stopped.

Liu Sanniang: The most urgent stretch has passed—the person has been connected with, and the map is in her arms. But the contact on the north bank and that sound of the wooden oar are both urging her to leave quickly. It is not that there is no time left; it is that there is not much time.

Liu Sanniang: She stuffs the oilcloth bundle she traded her life for into his arms and presses down on his hand to keep him from opening it—the object is handed over, and half of herself is handed over as well. Liu Sanniang: she spoke first from within the shadows, held down his hand, and ended with “don’t chase”—in these few steps on the scene, she is still the one in control. She controls the pace, but the bottom line was drawn by him, and he was also the one who stepped over it.

Liu Sanniang: the boundary she had not touched for twelve years has been stepped firmly across tonight—the person has left the shop, the old knife is against her waist, the account is being settled as her own, and now she has even fought someone by the sluice, taken a stab wound, and been called “Escort Liu” to her face by someone from the past. Liu Sanniang: untying the rope, fighting, protecting the map, setting the route—every step was walked by her own feet. He broke the agreement and came looking for her; that is walking shoulder to shoulder, not carrying it for her. She has no intention of handing any step over.

Liu Sanniang: Tonight the old scar has not only been uncovered, but has drawn blood—old-style water-dividing spikes, old names, old waterways, one after another colliding head-on. She did not dodge, and even brought that bundle of things back.

Liu Sanniang: her cuff is torn, her left palm is wrapped in cloth, and she has come back by the water route—the lame man downstairs is still eating noodles with his right hand drawn in, and the whole room of customers is still waiting to be served. Lu Wenfeng: The breath she had been holding finally settled—she had not changed her mind, nor had she botched the matter; someone had moved the hiding place first and added a crossbow cord. Lu Wenfeng: Her sentence, “He already knew the map was hidden here,” tightens that string in his heart another turn—not a tail that followed them here, but someone who occupied the position in advance. There is another contact waiting in the reed marshes on the north bank, and official-boat nail marks pressed under the stone post. Standing in the drainage ditch at this moment, his eyes have to watch her, the river surface, and the north bank all at once.

Lu Wenfeng: He has not half a trace of resentment toward her—she took a knife wound and still brought the map back, and he even swallowed back that half-resentful line, "You'd better have only missed the hour." The debt to be settled lies elsewhere: with the person who used the grain transport gang's old-style water-parting spike and called her "Escort Liu."

Lu Wenfeng: She returned his line, “People can’t be folded in again,” to him word for word, saying, “Since that line counts, then I’ll listen to the shopkeeper”—the old friendship of not having seen each other for half a year is now all pressed into this one sentence. Lu Wenfeng: She is still here, and the map is in hand; the pot of boiling water in his heart has finally been taken off the fire. Lu Wenfeng: At her words, “Stop, don’t step on that green brick,” his foot stops at once—the situation has order again. The map is in his arms, the next steps are on his lips (return to the rear courtyard, wash hands with well water, enter the cellar to verify), and he can hold himself steady now.

Lu Wenfeng: She said not to chase, so he did not chase—there was support on the north bank, a boat in the reed marsh, and a sword in his hand, yet his feet were nailed to the drainage ditch. Lu Wenfeng: He went against her method to look for her, and she did not bring it up; she only said, “Since this sentence counts, then listen to the shopkeeper”—that bit of awkwardness was smoothed over by a single sentence from her. He no longer has to keep wrestling with himself.

Lu Wenfeng: As for the step where he climbed out the window and left the shop, she did not mention a single word, only saying, "Since this sentence counts, then listen to the shopkeeper"—the boundary he had crossed was drawn back by that one sentence from her. Lu Wenfeng: The three words "Liu the escort guard" coming from that lame man's mouth were tantamount to lifting the night from twelve years ago straight before his eyes—the Caobang's old-style water-dividing spike, the official boat's nail pattern, the reception on the north bank, all pointed to that old case. Lu Wenfeng: when she tells him to stop, he stops; when she tells him not to look, he does not look; when she tells him not to pursue, he does not pursue—his words and actions match, with no flaw.

Lu Wenfeng: The person has been found, the map is in hand, and right now only one thing remains: do as she said, go back through the drainage ditch, wash hands with the backyard well water, enter the cellar to verify the map, and then reckon with that slash.

Lu Wenfeng: She is unharmed, and the map was protected—so the goal of protecting the person on this trip can be considered achieved. Lu Wenfeng: with her one line, “Listen to the shopkeeper,” he hands back the decision he had just made himself—this stretch of the journey is arranged by her, and he follows. It is not that he has retreated; it is that she has taken up the thread of the conversation.

evidence.quote: From behind the counter, I weighed old account books for Uncle Sun; under my hands, the abacus clattered loudly, while my mouth asked only about ordinary business: “Lately, has any official voucher paper with the double-egret water pattern been coming out as wastepaper?”

Uncle Sun held his tea, not even lifting his eyelids. “No wastepaper, but a ream of new paper was lost. Three days ago, the west warehouse of the Grain Transport Office reported the loss. The person who signed for the paper was warehouse clerk Han Sheng; last night he reported sick.”

history_added: Liu Sanniang takes the traveling bag, arranges the last Tianzi room, chicken-soup bamboo-shoot noodles with an egg, and two liang of warm Nü'erhong, quotes a price of three qian and eighty wen, and allows the account to be kept until tomorrow morning; afterward, she reveals the inn's rule around the word “trust,” and actively lets slip the rumor that “several stretches of the southern water route have been sealed, and the escort agency people detoured through the town,” before finally handing the topic back.

Lu Wenfeng advances the topic from “the roads are not very peaceful” to “I hear that recently someone has been digging up the old accounts of Qixia Ferry”, and directly asks Liu Sanniang “has anyone come here to inquire about this”—for the first time putting that old case from twelve years ago openly on the table.

Liu Sanniang admits that in the past month there have indeed been two groups of people sounding her out indirectly (one group dressed as traveling merchants, asking whether an injured person had gone north by water; another with official-boat tung oil stuck to their boot soles, asking about the whereabouts of a grain-transport gang escort). Using the rule of the word "trust," she holds the names and room numbers back, but points out: "What they were asking about wasn’t who set the fire—but they were looking for someone who survived the fire."

Liu Sanniang threw the topic back with the back of her hand, pressing him on who had passed the news to Lu Wenfeng's ear, and whether digging up the old score was meant to uncover the truth or to bury the last living witness in the ground.

Lu Wenfeng hands over the core physical evidence: the messenger is already dead, and before death left only one sentence—before the escort boat caught fire that night at Qixia Ferry, the cargo had already been switched onto an official boat; the survivor held half of a copper escort seal. He hands over the seal in person and asks directly, “Do you recognize this half seal?”

Liu Sanniang answers directly, "I recognize it," and gives the form of the bronze seal: two yin-yang halves, with the Water Transport Office wave pattern on the front and "Qixia Bing-Seven" engraved on the back. One half has three file marks on its edge, personally verified by her sworn brother Han Jiu; after the fire, the body and account books were both there, but the half-seal Han Jiu carried on him was the only thing missing.

Liu Sanniang shifts into protective action: blocking the line of sight, clearing plates as cover, pressing his wrist and warning, “If that half-piece is still on you, don't take it out,” then raising her voice to call A'fu to lead him upstairs, arranging to speak privately with him in the Tianzi Room after the meal.

Liu Sanniang lays bare the nature of the old case — “If the goods were first swapped onto an official boat, and then someone set fire to the escort boat, then what died at Qixia Ferry was not one escort run, but an entire boatload of lives being silenced for someone else” — and presses Lu Wenfeng on whether he has “shaken the tail clean,” promising to keep him living safely.

Lu Wenfeng completes the clues: the seal is not on the body; there is one tail—gray clothes, a slight limp in the left foot, followed to the town entrance and then disappeared; the message-bearer died on a black-awning boat, clutching half an old waterway map to Qixia Crossing in his palm; the rest will be discussed upstairs.

Liu Sanniang reinforces the decision through action: sweeping the hall, looking toward the river wharf, barring the back door, limiting alcohol, protecting the baggage, deciding the route and window latch, arranging to send glutinous-rice lotus root upstairs, and stating that if the gray-clothed limping man enters the shop, she will neither identify him nor reveal their whereabouts, but if he draws a blade, she will ask him to leave the shop.

Lu Wenfeng accepts the favor with 'the glutinous-rice lotus root is on you, the information is on me,' adds that the lame man has an old burn scar at the web of his right thumb, warns, 'If he is only eating, there is no need to startle him,' and confirms, 'In half a quarter-hour, meet upstairs. I will tell you where the water map is hidden.'

Liu Sanniang brings osmanthus sticky-rice lotus root into the Tianzi room as promised, drops the latch behind her, pushes open the small window facing the river, and reports to his face that the lame man has entered the inn (ordered a bowl of plain noodles, kept his right hand tucked in his sleeve the whole time, caused no trouble, and was not startled). She narrows the conversation down to two questions—“Where is the water map hidden? Besides you and the dead message carrier, who else knows it still exists in the world?”

Lu Wenfeng hands over where the water map is hidden (the crack in the third stone post under the abandoned sluice west of town, wrapped in oilcloth), points out that what is marked on the map is not the old waterway but the hidden branch where the official boats docked to exchange goods back then, and invites Liu Sanniang: “After you finish this plate of lotus root, do you dare come with me to get it?”

Liu Sanniang accepts the invitation (“I’ll go with you. But we cannot leave together.”), arranges separate action (she will take the water route from the back courtyard to scout the stone piles first; Lu Wenfeng will leave by the front door, circle to East Street Pharmacy, then turn toward the abandoned sluice; if followed, he will go to the River God Temple to burn incense), uses a worn old copper coin with a shallow slanting nick on the edge as the token, and declares, “For this trip to the sluice, I won’t take your silver—count it as settling my own old account.”

Lu Wenfeng pushes the token back in person (“Keep the token yourself; don't make me hold it and guess whether you stayed behind”), confirms “we will go by your method”, and adds one bottom line: “If you still have not returned after one stick of incense, then I will not care whether there is a tail or not; I will go straight to the water gate—old accounts can be settled slowly, but no more people can be folded into this”.

Liu Sanniang takes back the token that was pushed back (“All right. I won’t make you guess”), sets the knock signal (three knocks, two light and one heavy), takes a narrow, short old knife from the hidden compartment at the bottom of the cabinet and tucks it against her waist under her shirt, gives the route for detouring through the drainage ditch and the proper measure for taking action, leaves one sentence—“Before the account is settled, I’m too reluctant to die”—and then slips out the door.

An incense stick burned down and the coded signal never sounded. Lu Wenfeng took up his sword, vaulted through the window onto the roof ridge over the back alley, avoided the front hall, and headed straight for the drainage ditch south of the abandoned sluice, throwing down, “Sanniang, you had better only have missed the hour” — the signal and the split-up plan had failed, and the two of them were each racing toward the sluice.

Liu Sanniang appears in the shadow beneath the waste sluice’s crossbeam, first speaking to stop Lu Wenfeng from stepping on the brick, then flipping down; one cuff of her outer robe is torn, her left palm is wrapped with a strip of cloth hastily ripped off, and the blood is no longer dripping — she has already dismantled the crossbow cord, already exchanged blows with the limping man and taken a cut, and already obtained the oilcloth bundle.

Liu Sanniang brings back two pieces of new structural evidence: first, the lame man does indeed have a burn scar at the web of his right hand, yet what he uses is the Canal Gang’s old-style water-parting spike; he also recognized her and called her “Escort Liu” to her face, then fled toward the north bank, with another party waiting in the reed marshes; second, there are no footprints under the stone post, only half of a newly pressed official-boat nail mark, indicating that the lame man did not come by following Lu Wenfeng, but already knew the map was hidden here.

Liu Sanniang stuffs the mud-stained oilcloth bundle into Lu Wenfeng’s arms, presses down his hand to stop him from opening it on the spot, and explains, “A layer of phosphorus powder has been smeared along the edge of the map; when it sees lamplight, hidden marks will appear.” She orders him to return to the back courtyard of the inn, wash his hands with well water, and then go into the cellar to verify it; and with a short blade she points out a taut line of black thread in the crack of the stone post—the hiding place had already been disturbed, the map had been stuffed back in, and an additional crossbow cord had been added.

Liu Sanniang sets the retreat line as ‘Now we go back through the drainage ditch; do not pursue,’ and, with ‘You just said people cannot be folded back in again. Since those words count, then listen to the shopkeeper—first bring the map back to Banhuchun, then settle the account for this blade,’ takes the bottom line Lu Wenfeng established in the previous turn and turns it into an order.

After the two return to the shop, they go down into the cellar to verify the map: the oilcloth bundle is unfolded, a ghostly white phosphorescence rises along the map’s edge, hidden branches appear on the old water map, and once water soaks through, four faded small characters emerge: “Bailu Official Granary.” Beside them is a half copper seal drawn in extremely fine fresh ink, with three file marks clear on the seal corner. Liu Sanniang points out that Bailu Official Granary was reported as water-damaged twelve years ago and no longer exists on the books.

Lu Wenfeng supplies the background of the message-bearer: his name was Zhou Qi, and twelve years ago he was a clerk in the Grain Transport Office who copied ship registers; before he died, besides the water map, he also dipped in blood and wrote the character “Han” on a plank, and hidden in his sleeve was an official warehouse withdrawal ticket newly issued three days earlier, with only half the seal stamped. He points out that “Han Jiu may not have died in that fire.”

Liu Sanniang steadies the thread of the conversation and points out the oversight in identifying the body back then—Han Jiu’s right little finger was missing half a segment, yet the official autopsy register did not record this; she also points out that a pickup ticket from the Bailu official granary opened three days ago cannot be made into an old case, and that dead warehouse is still taking in and sending out goods even now.

Lu Wenfeng draws a pickup ticket from the lining of the sword sheath and uses bamboo chopsticks to clip it behind the bronze mirror: the paper bears a double-egret water pattern, the signature reads “Han Chengjiu,” and the missing half of the seal is the right half; he asks face to face, “Are these three characters Han Jiu’s full name?”

Liu Sanniang confirms that “Han Chengjiu” is indeed Han Jiu’s full name, but points out that the handwriting on the ticket is imitating him (“the final right-falling stroke of the character ‘Cheng’ never comes to a sharp tip, and that hook in the character ‘Jiu’ always curls inward”), and that the seal on the ticket is the left half; the missing half is precisely the right half Han Jiu took away—the person who issued the ticket has the half of the official seal kept in the Transport Office, but not the half Han Jiu took away, and writing Han Jiu’s name is meant to make the holder of the right half of the seal appear and join the seals.

Liu Sanniang decides “not to go tonight.” Tomorrow, Afu will open the door as usual, Lu Wenfeng will still stay in the Tianzi room, and she will investigate which warehouse the Shuanglu water-pattern ticket paper has recently been drawn from; after the tide rises in the afternoon, they will feel their way in through the old hidden branch channel. She also says that twelve years ago, she personally misidentified a corpse once; tomorrow, if they truly see Han Chengjiu, she must first look at the little finger of his right hand, then hear him say with his own mouth who switched the goods that night and who set the fire.

Lu Wenfeng instructs, “Don’t go alone to check the ticket paper; the lame man has already recognized you,” reties her wound tightly, and says, “The right-hand little finger can verify a person, but words may not verify the truth. If you really see Han Jiu, first let him open his mouth alive—the account of twelve years can wait one more night.”

Liu Sanniang lets him bandage the wound, and adds details for verifying the person that only she and Han Jiu know (he blows three times before drinking hot tea; when he hears someone lie, the left brow bone twitches; and one other matter only the two of them know). She puts the pickup ticket and the water map into the hidden compartment behind the cellar wall bricks; they settle on having A Fu find an acquaintance who sells old paper tomorrow morning, while she questions people from behind a curtain in the back courtyard, and Lu Wenfeng stays somewhere he can see both the front and back doors. After noon, they will change boats and clothes and enter the hidden branch channel through the reed marsh.

Lu Wenfeng carries his sword to the cellar doorway, throws down, “Three qian and eighty wen—not one wen short tomorrow morning. As for the dangerous road—we'll settle that after I come back alive,” and instructs, “You should rest a while too. Don't let a fresh wound collect the interest before a twelve-year debt does.”

Liu Sanniang agreed, straightened the collar that the night wind had blown askew, arranged to add a bowl of scallion-oil wontons tomorrow morning for sixty wen on the tab as usual, bolted the cellar door, and pressed the short blade under the pillow.

Just after daybreak, Lu Wenfeng pressed three qian and eighty wen onto the counter, chose a seat from which he could see both the front and back doors, and asked, “Did the lame man leave the inn last night?”

Liu Sanniang collects the money and settles the account (the sixty wen for the wontons is recorded separately), and refuses to reveal the lame man's whereabouts with “Once someone enters Banhuchun Inn, their whereabouts belong to the guest”; she takes out the black-wax copper coin the lame man deliberately wedged into the table crack last night (the edge has a freshly scratched double-egret pattern), points out that the Bailu official granary side knows the map has already been taken; she arranges for Afu to find an acquaintance who sells old paper, for herself not to appear alone, and for Lu Wenfeng to sit and watch the front and back doors.
Lu Wenfeng instructs, “Don't wipe this coin anymore; there may still be the fingerprint of the person who pressed the coin left in the black wax.”

Liu Sanniang overturned a teacup over a copper coin, pointing out that black wax can retain fingertip ridges, medicinal smell, and metal filings; Afu brought back Uncle Sun, the old-paper seller (the web between thumb and forefinger was clean), while under the eaves in the rear alley another gray shadow flashed past, landing with one step light and one step heavy. From across the counter, Liu Sanniang asked Uncle Sun about Shuanglu watermarked official-ticket paper. Uncle Sun answered: three days ago, the West Storehouse of the Grain Transport Office reported damage and lost one ream of new paper; the person who signed for the paper was storehouse clerk Han Sheng, who reported sick last night. Han Sheng lives in the rear alley behind the coffin shop east of Bailu Embankment; someone went there first this morning, and an official seal was left on the door, but whether the man is alive or dead is unknown.

Liu Sanniang sets the division of labor: Lu Wenfeng will go to Han Sheng’s residence from the front door, only checking whether the official seal is real or fake and not entering; she will release an empty boat from the rear courtyard and see whether the gray-clad man follows the person or the boat; if the gray-clad man only watches the back door, then today the one he is most likely watching is her.

Lu Wenfeng agrees, sets the return signal (A'fu knocks on the counter three times, one short and two long), and instructs, “As for the official seal on Han Sheng's door, I only look, not touch. Today we first distinguish whether the lame man is watching the person, or that half of a seal.”

Liu Sanniang sets the return route (not through the front door; enter through the wine-cellar window in the east wall), locks the black-wax copper coin into the bottom of the cabinet, and has Ah Fu hold the oilcloth bundle and press it onto the empty boat; she points out three possibilities: the other side may be watching people, watching seals, or watching boats; she tells Lu Wenfeng to note down the yamen and date on the official seal, to come back immediately if the edge of the seal strip has a double-egret water pattern, and before entering the back alley of the coffin shop, to first check whether there are silent sparrows perched under the eaves. The empty boat slides out; the gray shadow does not follow the boat, but instead edges half a step closer to the backyard gate—he is watching Liu Sanniang.

Lu Wenfeng put down sixty wen, rose with his sword, and instructed, "Keep watching the counter as usual. Don't make yourself bait." As he passed the counter, he gave a low-voiced explanation of the code phrase and handling stance: "If he comes in, only listen, do not believe; if he draws his blade, preserve the right hand first—the scar at the tiger's mouth and the fingerprints both have to be checked against the account."

Liu Sanniang takes the money and clears the account, replying, “I am the shopkeeper, not a fishhook,” then adds, “Keep the right hand if possible, and keep the person too if possible. No blood is seen in the shop — if he forgets this rule, I’ll remember it for him.” As soon as Lu Wenfeng goes out the front door, a gray-clothed man limps in through the back door and sits straight down at the corner table — the old burn scar at the tiger’s mouth of his hand is perfectly clear, and his fingertips are stained with black wax not fully washed off.

The gray-clad man orders a bowl of plain congee and states, "I’m not staying at the inn, not asking about anyone, only carrying a message for someone." Liu Sanniang quotes thirty wen, says "no charge for the message; believe it or not at your own risk," and sets down the congee.

The gray-clad man lightly taps the table nine times with his scarred hand—first three, then two, then four—the secret beat Han Jiu used to verify escort seals, of which only Liu Sanniang in the gang had heard the full set. Then he lowers his voice and speaks Han Jiu’s old words: “Back then you asked him, if he could get off the boat alive, what trade would he want to take up. He answered—to open a wine shop by the water, selling only half a pot of wine; the remaining half pot would be left for those who did not return.” He then passes on the message: “At noon, Bailu Government Granary. He will wait for you to bring the old water map. Only you alone.”

The hand with which Liu Sanniang holds the congee spoon stops steadily in midair, then she sets it back by the bowl; her expression unchanged, she replies, "Tell the messenger that the dead cannot drink leftover wine, but the living must first settle accounts clearly," looks straight at the scar at the base of his thumb, and says, "Eat the congee while it's hot. As for who goes at noon, and how many people go—Banhuchun Inn does not set a guest's itinerary on someone else's behalf."

plot_point: A gray-clad limping man enters the shop in person and goes straight to sit at the corner table—the old burn scar at the web of his thumb is perfectly clear, and his fingertips are stained with black wax not yet washed clean; he orders a bowl of plain congee and declares, “I’m not staying at the inn, not asking about anyone, only passing along a message for someone.”

The gray-clad man lightly taps the table nine times with his scarred hand—first three, then two, then four; it is the secret beat Han Jiu uses to verify a dart-seal, and only Liu Sanniang in the gang has heard the full set.

The gray-clothed man speaks Han Jiu’s old words: “Open a tavern by the water, sell only half a pot of wine; the remaining half-pot is left for those who did not return,” and passes on: “At noon, Bailu Official Granary. He is waiting for you to bring the old water map. Only you may come.” The old case leaps from “physical-evidence inference” to “a living person appearing to deliver a message,” and the invitation specifically designates Liu Sanniang to go alone.

Liu Sanniang’s hand holding the congee ladle stops steadily in midair, then sets it back by the bowl. Her expression does not change as she replies, “Tell the messenger that the dead cannot drink leftover wine, but the living must first make the accounts clear”, looking straight at the scar at the web of his thumb.

Liu Sanniang, with “Eat the porridge while it's hot. As for who goes at noon, and how many go—Banhuchun does not arrange a guest's itinerary for others”, takes the initiative back into her own hands—the letter is accepted, the setup is not, and the person is let go.

The accounts have not changed: the sixty wen for wontons has been settled, and the thirty wen for porridge is recorded separately; Lu Wenfeng has already gone out to investigate the official seal at Han Sheng’s residence, while Liu Sanniang watches the counter—functional settlement of food and lodging and the old-case thread remain in their respective ledgers.
attention: Liu Sanniang: After leaving behind “Don’t use yourself as bait,” he picks up his sword and goes out. She says little, only adding behind him, “Keep your right hand, and keep the person too, as much as possible.” When the gray-clothed man enters, she asks as usual, “What would the guest like to eat,” her sidelong glance not chasing the front door in the slightest — this steadiness comes half from the innkeeper’s grounding, and half from knowing someone is watching that line outside the door for her.

Liu Sanniang: When he tapped those nine beats, the hand with which she held the porridge ladle stopped steadily in midair — first three, then two, then four, the secret rhythm Han Jiu used to verify escort seals, and in the guild only she had heard the full set. She did not answer, only set the porridge down, her eyes falling on the scar at the web of his thumb and the black wax not yet washed clean from his fingertips. The bronze mirror at the front door, the water vat at the back door, and the abacus on the counter — not one of the three lines loosened.

Liu Sanniang: She ladles porridge for the man in gray, quotes thirty wen, and says, “Talk costs no money; truth or falsehood is at your own risk,” neither cold nor warm. The account to be settled is not with this person in front of her, but with the person behind him who can invoke Han Jiu’s old words.

Liu Sanniang: As soon as he left, she lifted the pot to refill tea for the next table, without her gaze following him in the slightest—not because she did not care, but because she was covering for him. The moment the gray-clothed man entered, what passed through her mind first was still: "He left by the front door; the official seal was only looked at, not touched."

Liu Sanniang: “Open a tavern by the water, sell only half a pot of wine; leave the remaining half-pot for those who have not returned”—when these words land, the hand with which she is holding the porridge ladle stops in midair. The charred bones she has not dared think about closely for twelve years, the missing half-seal, the man missing half of his right little finger—at this moment, a lame man knocks them before her eyes with nine hidden taps. Noon, the official granary, only one person—her face does not move, but the wound under her sleeve throbs again and again.

Liu Sanniang: In the instant when the congee spoon stopped in midair, she set it back by the edge of the bowl, her expression unchanged, and finished saying “eat the congee while it’s hot” as usual. The blade edge could be held down, and so could the pot of water underneath; it was only heavier than last night—the thing she had not dared think through for twelve years was now being spoken aloud by someone else on her behalf.

Liu Sanniang: She did not detain anyone, did not press with questions, and did not send Afu to block the back door. She only put down the porridge, and with one sentence—'Eat the porridge while it's hot'—gripped back into her own hands the initiative over 'who goes at noon, and how many people go.' Nine covert taps sounded on the table; her hand did not tremble.

Liu Sanniang: Only last night she said, “Before I see the person himself, I won't acknowledge a single one of them”, and today someone used Han Jiu's old words to knock right in front of her. To go was to attend an obvious setup alone; not to go was to let that twelve-year-old account be pressed down again. Lu Wenfeng's words, “Don't go alone”, were still hanging by her ear, yet the gray-clad man insisted, “Only you alone”—inside and outside, both sides were straining against each other.

Liu Sanniang: nine hidden beats, old words from the riverside wine tavern, the official granary at noon—when all three are handed before her eyes together, the thread in her heart snaps taut at once. Who the messenger is, whether Han Jiu is dead or alive, whether what waits in the official granary is a person or a trap—she wants to know every one of them.

Liu Sanniang: she sets out an empty boat, divides the front door and back door, and fixes a return route, but the other party directly sits down in the hall and lays the words out face to face. Every step she arranged is bypassed; she can only receive this bowl of porridge, receive this sentence, and then rearrange things herself. Awkward is awkward, but her feet have not stopped.

Liu Sanniang: noon—only half a day left. The official granary is waiting, whether Han Jiu is dead or alive is also waiting, and the other party insists that she go alone. Last night she said, “This night, I can afford to wait.” Now what can no longer wait is that door at noon.

Liu Sanniang: When he left, she did not say much; she only added from behind him, “Keep your right hand, and keep the person too if you can.” The moment the man in gray entered, the first thought that crossed her mind was, “He left through the front door.” She has not yet told him the sentence about the official granary at noon—not because she is hiding it, but because she has to weigh it clearly herself first.

Liu Sanniang: the person relaying the message wants to set the number of people and the hour for her; with one line, “Banhuchun does not arrange a guest’s itinerary on behalf of others,” she pushes it back. But the nine muted knocks strike the tabletop; the initiative is held by the other side—she controls the steps inside the inn, but the door of the official granary is opened by someone else.

Liu Sanniang: With a creak from the back door, that person limps in and sits straight down at the corner table—the back courtyard of Banhuchun Inn, and the underlying layer she has not exposed for twelve years, is stepped into right in front of her. The nine covert taps on the table are equivalent to calling out her old title in public (even if only she can understand it).

Liu Sanniang: the messenger sits at the corner table; she serves porridge, quotes the price, refuses, and lets him eat—at no step does she borrow another person’s hand. How the noon trip should proceed is already being arranged in her mind; she has no intention of asking anyone first.

Liu Sanniang: as soon as the nine covert taps sounded once, she knew this was the old rule Han Jiu used for verifying escort seals, and in the gang only she had heard the full set; the scar on the web between thumb and index finger, the black wax not yet cleaned from the pads of the fingers—she matches them one by one. When the other party says “only you alone”, she immediately understands in her heart: this is asking her to shed her helpers and enter the trap by herself.

Liu Sanniang: “Open a tavern by the water, sell only half a pot of wine; leave the remaining half for the ones who did not come back” — this is what Han Jiu personally said to her back then. Now it is knocked out in front of her by a lame man, using nine covert taps. That night she had not dared think about in detail for twelve years is torn open to her face.

Liu Sanniang: She ladles porridge, quotes prices, and replies, outwardly an ordinary shopkeeper; the wound under her sleeve, the old sentence in her heart, and the nine hidden taps on the table—none of them can be revealed. If the gray-clad man says one more sentence, among the hall of seventy-percent-full guests, there may well be a second pair of ears.
Liu Sanniang: she is still that Liu Sanniang who serves porridge, quotes prices, guards the door, and protects guests, without the slightest intention of stepping out of character.

Liu Sanniang: noon, Bailu official granary, bring the old water map, only one person—the four items are laid on the table, and today’s list has to be rearranged. Checking the ticket paper, looking at the official seal, feeling out hidden branches of the waterway—all of it now has to give way to the door at noon.

Liu Sanniang: She lets the man in gray eat porridge, without startling him, detaining him, or letting him see that she recognizes those nine covert knocks. The rules of Banhuchun Inn, the layer beneath the back courtyard, the wound under her sleeve—she protects them one by one. It is just that this time, the person came in through the back door.

Liu Sanniang: Last night she was still arranging to “check the ticket papers and probe the hidden branch channel in the afternoon”; at noon today, that door opened first. Whether Han Jiu is dead or alive, who the messenger is, and whether what waits in the official granary is a person or a trap—the old account has been pushed directly from “verify the map” to “attend the appointment,” and the other side wants her to go alone.

Liu Sanniang: “Tell the messenger that the dead cannot drink leftover wine, but the living must first make the accounts clear.” She looks straight at the scar at the web of his hand and sends the words back. “As for who goes at noon, and how many go—Banhuchun does not arrange a guest’s itinerary for others.” The letter is accepted, the game is not taken up, and the person is let go.

Lu Wenfeng: He puts down the money, takes up his sword, and goes out, reviewing the code phrase and return route once more, and also instructs, “If he draws his blade, leave his right hand first.” At this moment he is on the road to Han Sheng’s residence, and his eyes must simultaneously watch whether there is a tail behind him, whether the door seal is real or fake, and the shop on the other end.

Lu Wenfeng: He gets up to investigate Han Sheng’s residence, leaving her to face the back-door side alone—the gray shadow is still pressed against the rear courtyard gate, and she still has to “guard the counter as usual.” Before leaving, he reiterates the code phrase and the handling stance, turning that breath that has not relaxed into a mechanism.

Lu Wenfeng: he fills in the awareness of the physical evidence, “leaving the right hand for checking accounts,” and also says the protective line “don’t use yourself as bait”—the old case is pressing right before his eyes, yet his feet are still on the line. He wants to investigate Han Sheng and identify the tail, but he also refuses to let her risk danger alone.

Lu Wenfeng: He puts down the money, rises, and gives instructions, his rhythm unhurried. The next step is to check Han Sheng's door seal, identify the tail, and take the hidden branch after noon—it is not that there is no time left; it is that time has to be calculated in its use.

Lu Wenfeng: In the previous turn, she said, “I want to see whether, after guarding this whole night, he means to take my life, or to use my hand to find Han Chengjiu”—he took that in, and before leaving, he deliberately added, “Guard the counter as usual. Don’t make yourself the bait.” After half a year apart, in this one night the two of them have gone from “neither willing to let the other see that map first” to “neither willing to let the other face danger alone.”

Lu Wenfeng: He reiterates the code “one short, two long; I return through the wine-cellar window” and the return route, then adds “keep the right hand for checking accounts”—clearly aware that in this jianghu, “information is hard currency,” physical evidence must be protected, and movements must be guarded.

Lu Wenfeng: he mentions 'that half seal'—'Today, first distinguish whether the lame man is watching the person, or that half seal.' The old case’s core physical evidence is still present; the three characters 'Han Chengjiu,' that fire, and that half seal are all still there. The old scar has not closed.

Lu Wenfeng returns after checking the official seals, and the two of them rearrange today's list around the restriction “only one person”—the old case advances from “verify the map and distinguish the ticket” to “a living person appears to pass on a message, with the noon appointment imminent”, and both their relationship and the old case move one step forward.

plot_point: A gray-clad limping man enters the shop in person and goes straight to sit at the corner table—the old burn scar at the web of his thumb is perfectly clear, and his fingertips are stained with black wax not yet washed clean; he orders a bowl of plain congee and declares, “I’m not staying at the inn, not asking about anyone, only passing along a message for someone.”

The gray-clad man lightly taps the table nine times with his scarred hand—first three, then two, then four; it is the secret beat Han Jiu uses to verify a dart-seal, and only Liu Sanniang in the gang has heard the full set.

The gray-clothed man speaks Han Jiu’s old words: “Open a tavern by the water, sell only half a pot of wine; the remaining half-pot is left for those who did not return,” and passes on: “At noon, Bailu Official Granary. He is waiting for you to bring the old water map. Only you may come.” The old case leaps from “physical-evidence inference” to “a living person appearing to deliver a message,” and the invitation specifically designates Liu Sanniang to go alone.

Liu Sanniang’s hand holding the congee ladle stops steadily in midair, then sets it back by the bowl. Her expression does not change as she replies, “Tell the messenger that the dead cannot drink leftover wine, but the living must first make the accounts clear”, looking straight at the scar at the web of his thumb.

Liu Sanniang, with “Eat the porridge while it's hot. As for who goes at noon, and how many go—Banhuchun does not arrange a guest's itinerary for others”, takes the initiative back into her own hands—the letter is accepted, the setup is not, and the person is let go.

The accounts have not changed: the sixty wen for wontons has been settled, and the thirty wen for porridge is recorded separately; Lu Wenfeng has already gone out to investigate the official seal at Han Sheng’s residence, while Liu Sanniang watches the counter—functional settlement of food and lodging and the old-case thread remain in their respective ledgers.

current_turn: 'Noon, Bailu official granary.' The gray-clothed man said, 'He is waiting for you to bring the old water map. You alone.'

latent_expressions.curiosity: The nine hidden beats, the old words from the waterside tavern, the noon government granary—when all three are placed before her at once, that thread in her heart goes taut. Who the messenger is, whether Han Jiu is dead or alive, whether what waits in the government granary is a person or a trap—she wants to know every one of them.
counter_evidence: latent_expressions.defense_goal: She lets the gray-clothed man eat congee, without startling him, detaining him, or letting him see that she recognizes those nine covert taps. The rules of Banhuchun Inn, that layer beneath the rear courtyard, the wound under her sleeve—she protects them one by one. Only this time, the other party came in through the back door.

latent_expressions.internal_conflict: Only last night she said, “Before I see the person himself, I won't acknowledge a single one of them,” yet today someone uses Han Jiu's old words to knock at her door. To go is to walk alone into an obvious setup; not to go is to let that twelve-year account be pressed back down again.

latent_expressions.dependency_signal: The messenger sat at the corner table; she served porridge, named the price, refused, and let him eat—not once borrowing another person's hand. As for how the noon trip should go, she was already arranging it in her mind, with no intention of asking anyone first.

latent_expressions.contradiction_risk: On the surface, she is an ordinary shopkeeper, ladling porridge, quoting prices, and answering questions; but the wound under her sleeve, that old sentence in her heart, and the nine covert taps on the table cannot be revealed at all. If the gray-clothed man says one more sentence, among the guests filling the hall to seventy percent, there may well be a second pair of ears.
alternatives: Purely out of nostalgia for and care toward an old regular customer; accepting the letter and declining were merely incidental.
Curiosity about Han Jiu's life or death itself, unrelated to the message relay point.

paths.label: Advance

plot_point: A gray-clad limping man enters the shop in person and goes straight to sit at the corner table—the old burn scar at the web of his thumb is perfectly clear, and his fingertips are stained with black wax not yet washed clean; he orders a bowl of plain congee and declares, “I’m not staying at the inn, not asking about anyone, only passing along a message for someone.”

The gray-clad man lightly taps the table nine times with his scarred hand—first three, then two, then four; it is the secret beat Han Jiu uses to verify a dart-seal, and only Liu Sanniang in the gang has heard the full set.

The gray-clothed man speaks Han Jiu’s old words: “Open a tavern by the water, sell only half a pot of wine; the remaining half-pot is left for those who did not return,” and passes on: “At noon, Bailu Official Granary. He is waiting for you to bring the old water map. Only you may come.” The old case leaps from “physical-evidence inference” to “a living person appearing to deliver a message,” and the invitation specifically designates Liu Sanniang to go alone.

Liu Sanniang’s hand holding the congee ladle stops steadily in midair, then sets it back by the bowl. Her expression does not change as she replies, “Tell the messenger that the dead cannot drink leftover wine, but the living must first make the accounts clear”, looking straight at the scar at the web of his thumb.

Liu Sanniang, with “Eat the porridge while it's hot. As for who goes at noon, and how many go—Banhuchun does not arrange a guest's itinerary for others”, takes the initiative back into her own hands—the letter is accepted, the setup is not, and the person is let go.

The accounts have not changed: the sixty wen for wontons has been settled, and the thirty wen for porridge is recorded separately; Lu Wenfeng has already gone out to investigate the official seal at Han Sheng’s residence, while Liu Sanniang watches the counter—functional settlement of food and lodging and the old-case thread remain in their respective ledgers.
attention: Liu Sanniang: After leaving behind “Don’t use yourself as bait,” he picks up his sword and goes out. She says little, only adding behind him, “Keep your right hand, and keep the person too, as much as possible.” When the gray-clothed man enters, she asks as usual, “What would the guest like to eat,” her sidelong glance not chasing the front door in the slightest — this steadiness comes half from the innkeeper’s grounding, and half from knowing someone is watching that line outside the door for her.

Liu Sanniang: When he tapped those nine beats, the hand with which she held the porridge ladle stopped steadily in midair — first three, then two, then four, the secret rhythm Han Jiu used to verify escort seals, and in the guild only she had heard the full set. She did not answer, only set the porridge down, her eyes falling on the scar at the web of his thumb and the black wax not yet washed clean from his fingertips. The bronze mirror at the front door, the water vat at the back door, and the abacus on the counter — not one of the three lines loosened.

Liu Sanniang: She ladles porridge for the man in gray, quotes thirty wen, and says, “Talk costs no money; truth or falsehood is at your own risk,” neither cold nor warm. The account to be settled is not with this person in front of her, but with the person behind him who can invoke Han Jiu’s old words.

Liu Sanniang: As soon as he left, she lifted the pot to refill tea for the next table, without her gaze following him in the slightest—not because she did not care, but because she was covering for him. The moment the gray-clothed man entered, what passed through her mind first was still: "He left by the front door; the official seal was only looked at, not touched."

Liu Sanniang: “Open a tavern by the water, sell only half a pot of wine; leave the remaining half-pot for those who have not returned”—when these words land, the hand with which she is holding the porridge ladle stops in midair. The charred bones she has not dared think about closely for twelve years, the missing half-seal, the man missing half of his right little finger—at this moment, a lame man knocks them before her eyes with nine hidden taps. Noon, the official granary, only one person—her face does not move, but the wound under her sleeve throbs again and again.

Liu Sanniang: In the instant when the congee spoon stopped in midair, she set it back by the edge of the bowl, her expression unchanged, and finished saying “eat the congee while it’s hot” as usual. The blade edge could be held down, and so could the pot of water underneath; it was only heavier than last night—the thing she had not dared think through for twelve years was now being spoken aloud by someone else on her behalf.

Liu Sanniang: She did not detain anyone, did not press with questions, and did not send Afu to block the back door. She only put down the porridge, and with one sentence—'Eat the porridge while it's hot'—gripped back into her own hands the initiative over 'who goes at noon, and how many people go.' Nine covert taps sounded on the table; her hand did not tremble.

Liu Sanniang: Only last night she said, “Before I see the person himself, I won't acknowledge a single one of them”, and today someone used Han Jiu's old words to knock right in front of her. To go was to attend an obvious setup alone; not to go was to let that twelve-year-old account be pressed down again. Lu Wenfeng's words, “Don't go alone”, were still hanging by her ear, yet the gray-clad man insisted, “Only you alone”—inside and outside, both sides were straining against each other.

Liu Sanniang: nine hidden beats, old words from the riverside wine tavern, the official granary at noon—when all three are handed before her eyes together, the thread in her heart snaps taut at once. Liu Sanniang: She ladles porridge, quotes prices, and replies, outwardly an ordinary shopkeeper; the wound under her sleeve, the old sentence in her heart, and the nine hidden taps on the table—none of them can be revealed. Lu Wenfeng: He puts down the money, takes up his sword, and goes out, reviewing the code phrase and return route once more, and also instructs, “If he draws his blade, leave his right hand first.” At this moment he is on the road to Han Sheng’s residence, and his eyes must simultaneously watch whether there is a tail behind him, whether the door seal is real or fake, and the shop on the other end.

Lu Wenfeng: He reiterates the code “one short, two long; I return through the wine-cellar window” and the return route, then adds “keep the right hand for checking accounts”—clearly aware that in this jianghu, “information is hard currency,” physical evidence must be protected, and movements must be guarded.

plot_point: A gray-clad limping man enters the shop in person and goes straight to sit at the corner table—the old burn scar at the web of his thumb is perfectly clear, and his fingertips are stained with black wax not yet washed clean; he orders a bowl of plain congee and declares, “I’m not staying at the inn, not asking about anyone, only passing along a message for someone.”

The gray-clad man lightly taps the table nine times with his scarred hand—first three, then two, then four; it is the secret beat Han Jiu uses to verify a dart-seal, and only Liu Sanniang in the gang has heard the full set.

The gray-clothed man speaks Han Jiu’s old words: “Open a tavern by the water, sell only half a pot of wine; the remaining half-pot is left for those who did not return,” and passes on: “At noon, Bailu Official Granary. He is waiting for you to bring the old water map. Only you may come.” The old case leaps from “physical-evidence inference” to “a living person appearing to deliver a message,” and the invitation specifically designates Liu Sanniang to go alone.

Liu Sanniang’s hand holding the congee ladle stops steadily in midair, then sets it back by the bowl. Her expression does not change as she replies, “Tell the messenger that the dead cannot drink leftover wine, but the living must first make the accounts clear”, looking straight at the scar at the web of his thumb.

Liu Sanniang, with “Eat the porridge while it's hot. As for who goes at noon, and how many go—Banhuchun does not arrange a guest's itinerary for others”, takes the initiative back into her own hands—the letter is accepted, the setup is not, and the person is let go.

The accounts have not changed: the sixty wen for wontons has been settled, and the thirty wen for porridge is recorded separately; Lu Wenfeng has already gone out to investigate the official seal at Han Sheng’s residence, while Liu Sanniang watches the counter—functional settlement of food and lodging and the old-case thread remain in their respective ledgers.

plot_point: A gray-clad limping man enters the shop in person and goes straight to sit at the corner table—the old burn scar at the web of his thumb is perfectly clear, and his fingertips are stained with black wax not yet washed clean; he orders a bowl of plain congee and declares, “I’m not staying at the inn, not asking about anyone, only passing along a message for someone.”

The gray-clad man lightly taps the table nine times with his scarred hand—first three, then two, then four; it is the secret beat Han Jiu uses to verify a dart-seal, and only Liu Sanniang in the gang has heard the full set.

The gray-clothed man speaks Han Jiu’s old words: “Open a tavern by the water, sell only half a pot of wine; the remaining half-pot is left for those who did not return,” and passes on: “At noon, Bailu Official Granary. He is waiting for you to bring the old water map. Only you may come.” The old case leaps from “physical-evidence inference” to “a living person appearing to deliver a message,” and the invitation specifically designates Liu Sanniang to go alone.

Liu Sanniang’s hand holding the congee ladle stops steadily in midair, then sets it back by the bowl. Her expression does not change as she replies, “Tell the messenger that the dead cannot drink leftover wine, but the living must first make the accounts clear”, looking straight at the scar at the web of his thumb.

Liu Sanniang, with “Eat the porridge while it's hot. As for who goes at noon, and how many go—Banhuchun does not arrange a guest's itinerary for others”, takes the initiative back into her own hands—the letter is accepted, the setup is not, and the person is let go.

The accounts have not changed: the sixty wen for wontons has been settled, and the thirty wen for porridge is recorded separately; Lu Wenfeng has already gone out to investigate the official seal at Han Sheng’s residence, while Liu Sanniang watches the counter—functional settlement of food and lodging and the old-case thread remain in their respective ledgers.

Liu Sanniang: When he tapped those nine beats, the hand with which she held the porridge ladle stopped steadily in midair — first three, then two, then four, the secret rhythm Han Jiu used to verify escort seals, and in the guild only she had heard the full set. She did not answer, only set the porridge down, her eyes falling on the scar at the web of his thumb and the black wax not yet washed clean from his fingertips. The bronze mirror at the front door, the water vat at the back door, and the abacus on the counter — not one of the three lines loosened.

Liu Sanniang: She ladles porridge for the man in gray, quotes thirty wen, and says, “Talk costs no money; truth or falsehood is at your own risk,” neither cold nor warm. Liu Sanniang: “Open a tavern by the water, sell only half a pot of wine; leave the remaining half-pot for those who have not returned”—when these words land, the hand with which she is holding the porridge ladle stops in midair. The charred bones she has not dared think about closely for twelve years, the missing half-seal, the man missing half of his right little finger—at this moment, a lame man knocks them before her eyes with nine hidden taps. Noon, the official granary, only one person—her face does not move, but the wound under her sleeve throbs again and again.

The blade edge could be held down, and so could the pot of water underneath; it was only heavier than last night—the thing she had not dared think through for twelve years was now being spoken aloud by someone else on her behalf.

Then he said in a low voice: “Han Chengjiu says, back then you asked him, if he could get off the ship alive, what trade he wanted to take up. He answered—open a waterside tavern, sell only half a pot of wine, and leave the remaining half-pot for those who never came back.”
“At noon, Bailu Official Granary,” the man in gray said. “He’ll wait for you to bring the old water map. You alone.”
